en: He cooks the *brahmaudana* (the food of Brahman); verily, he thereby bestows seed. With the clarified butter that remains, he anoints the halter and takes it up; for clarified butter is brilliance, and the horse belongs to Prajāpati; he thus endows Prajāpati with brilliance.
Indeed, this horse is unpurified and impure. 13.1.1. [2]

The girdle is made of *darbha* grass; for *darbha* is a means of purification (*pavitra*). It purifies him; thus he seizes one who is already purified and fit for sacrifice. When the horse was seized for sacrifice, its seed issued forth and became gold—namely, that which is gold.
He gives gold; verily he endows the horse with seed.

Prajāpati created the sacrifice; its greatness departed from it and entered the great officiating priests (*mahartvijas*). He sought it through the great officiating priests and found it through the great officiating priests. Therefore, the great officiating priests [eat] the *brahmaudana*.

They partake of the very greatness of the sacrifice; thus the sacrificer secures it for himself. He gives gold in the *brahmaudana* (the Brahmin’s rice-porridge). Rice-porridge is indeed seed, and gold is seed; verily, by means of seed he places seed within him. It consists of a hundred *mānas*;
man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundredfold power; verily, he bestows life, power, and vigor upon himself.
At the midday pressing, he takes four *vasatīvarī* waters; these have been brought together from all the quarters.
Food is indeed in the quarters, and water is food; verily, by means of food, he secures food for him.
Whatever part of the sacrifice is performed without a formula (*yajus*) is indeed unsuccessful.
With the verse, "They have taken this rein of the Truth," he takes up the horse's halter for the sake of performing the *yajus* and for the prosperity of the sacrifice.
It is twelve cubits long; the year has twelve months; verily, he attains the year-long sacrifice.
Regarding this they say: "Should the rein be made twelve cubits long, or thirteen cubits? This bull among the seasons is indeed the thirteenth month.
The year has thirteen months; this horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), which is the bull among sacrifices, is its summit.
Just as there is a hump on a bull, so is there a summit for this [sacrifice]. One should add a thirteenth cubit to the girth-rope; that is just like the hump of a bull being formed. 13.1.2. [3]
"Thou art Abhidhā"—therefore the performer of the Aśvamedha conquers all the quarters; "Thou art Bhuvana"—he thus conquers the world;
"Thou art the Controller, the Sustainer"—he thus makes him a controller and a sustainer; "Do thou go to Agni Vaiśvānara"—he thus causes him to go to Agni Vaiśvānara; "Go to the far-extending one."

Verily, he causes him to expand with offspring and cattle. With the words "Svāhā! this is his *vaṣaṭ*-call. With the words "May you go well to the gods," he makes him go well to the gods. With the words "To Prajāpati," since the horse belongs to Prajāpati, he endows it with its own deity. 13.1.2 [4]
He who binds the horse without having announced it to the Brahman and to the gods is liable to meet with misfortune.
He addresses the Brahman, saying: "O Brahman, I shall bind the horse for the gods and for Prajāpati; may I prosper thereby.
Having thus addressed the Brahman, he binds it for the sake of the Brahman alone; he does not meet with misfortune. Him [he addresses].
"Bind it for the gods, for Prajāpati; through that, may you prosper," thus the Brahman gives the impulse.
He thereby endows it with its own deity. Then he sprinkles it; the significance of this is the same as before.
He sprinkles it, saying, "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Prajāpati. Prajāpati, indeed, is the most powerful among the gods.
He bestows vigor upon it; therefore, among animals, the horse is the most vigorous.
"I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Indra and Agni"—Indra and Agni are indeed the most powerful among the gods;
he thus bestows power upon it, and therefore, among animals, the horse is the most powerful.

"I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Vāyu"—Vāyu is indeed the swiftest of the gods; verily, he bestows speed upon it. Therefore, among animals, the horse is the swiftest. "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to all the gods"—the All-gods are indeed the most glorious of the gods.

He bestows glory upon this [horse]; therefore, the horse is the most glorious of animals. "I sprinkle you, who are acceptable to all the gods," he says. Regarding this, they say: "Since the horse belongs to Prajāpati, why then does he sprinkle it for other deities? [The answer is: It is indeed all [the gods].
The deities are inherent in the Aśvamedha. When he says, "I sprinkle thee for all the gods," he thereby causes all the deities to be inherent in him;

therefore, all the deities are inherent in the Aśvamedha. Verily, evil seeks to seize him who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice. The horse is a thunderbolt. [He recites: "Far from here is the mortal, far the dog!"—[thereby] he drives away the dog.
Having killed the four-eyed dog, he causes it to float beneath the horse's feet; verily, he tramples it with the thunderbolt, and no evil rival reaches him.
Just as the oblation might spill before it is offered, so does that animal spill which [he fails to treat thus]. 13.1.3. [1]

They discard what has been offered but not yet reached [the fire]; that which he offers in small portions (stokīya) ensures that he offers it as a complete oblation (sarvahuta) so that nothing is spilled, for that which spills from what has been offered is indeed not spilled. He offers a thousand;
the heavenly world is commensurate with a thousand, for the conquest of the heavenly world. 13.1.3. [2]

Regarding this they say: "If one were to offer measured oblations, he would obtain only the limited. Therefore, he offers unmeasured oblations for the sake of obtaining the unlimited. Prajāpati indeed said: "In the *stokīya* verses, I establish the Aśvamedha;
once it is thus established, I proceed from that point onward. 13.1.3. [3]
With "Svāhā to Agni," he offers it to Agni; with "Svāhā to Soma," he offers it to Soma;

with "Svāhā to the joy of the waters," he offers it to the waters; with "Svāhā to Savitṛ," he offers it to Savitṛ; with "Svāhā to Vāyu," he offers it to Vāyu; with "Svāhā to Viṣṇu," he offers it to Viṣṇu; [with] "Svāhā to Indra" [he offers it to Indra].
With "Svāhā to Indra," he offers it indeed to Indra; with "Svāhā to Bṛhaspati," he offers it indeed to Bṛhaspati;
with "Svāhā to Mitra," he offers it indeed to Mitra; with "Svāhā to Varuṇa," he offers it indeed to Varuṇa.
So many indeed are all the gods; to them he offers it. He offers [the oblations] directed away; for the heavenly world is, as it were, turned away; [this is] for the sake of the heavenly world.
For the conquest of the world. 13.1.3.[4] He who offers oblations directed away is liable to burn away from this world; he turns back again and becomes firmly established in this very world.
He indeed declared this to be the completion of the sacrifice, so that nothing may be spilled—for what has been spilled is lost.
Now, as to why that which has been offered spills over:

just as the oblation might spill over before it is offered, so does this animal spill over when they release one that has been sprinkled but not yet slaughtered. When he offers the *rūpas*, he makes it a complete offering.
He offers [the oblation] so that it does not spill, for that which spills from what has been offered does not spill [in this case]. "To the *hiṅ* (the sound *hiṅ*), svāhā!
To the one for whom the *hiṅ* has been made, svāhā!"—these indeed are the forms of the horse; verily, he thereby wins them. Regarding this they say:
"The forms are indeed no offering; these should not be offered. But then they also say: "In this very [act], the Aśvamedha is present."

"He establishes [the view]: 'Since he offers the *rūpas*, they must indeed be offered. Verily, for him who offers oblations elsewhere than in the fire—that is, outside its proper place—he deprives him of his abode and brings forth an enemy against him.
(13.1.3) Having recited [the formulas] prior to the Sāvitrī sacrifice itself, he offers the *rūpas* all at once into the Āhavanīya fire; this is their proper place.
He offers these oblations; he does not produce a rival for him. He offers at each beginning of the sacrifice for the continuity and non-interruption of the sacrifice.
Regarding this they say: "If one were to offer at each beginning of the sacrifice, he would be deprived of his cattle."
If one were to become worse off, he should offer [the oblations] only once; he is not deprived of cattle, nor does he become worse off.

He offers forty-eight [oblations]; the Jagatī meter has forty-eight syllables, and cattle are of the nature of the Jagatī; verily by means of the Jagatī he secures cattle for him. He offers one extra [oblation]; therefore, among offspring, one man is preeminent. 13.1.4. [1]
Prajāpati created the Aśvamedha; once created, it went away from him and entered the quarters. The gods sought it out;
they pursued it with *iṣṭi* offerings, they sought it with *iṣṭi* offerings, and they found it with *iṣṭi* offerings. When one sacrifices with *iṣṭis*, he thereby makes the horse fit for sacrifice.
The sacrificer follows after [the cows].
(13.1.4) There are verses addressed to Savitṛ; for Savitṛ is this earth. Whosoever hides upon her or goes elsewhere, it is indeed on her that they find him.
No one—neither horizontally nor upwards—is able to pass beyond this earth; such is the nature of the verses addressed to Savitṛ.

[These offerings] are for the sake of following after the horse itself. Regarding this, they say: "The horse is indeed lost when it goes away facing the opposite direction, for they do not bring it back. In that he offers the *dhṛti* oblations in the evening—since security (*kṣema*) is indeed *dhṛti*, and the night is security—he supports it with security; therefore [he offers them] in the evening.

Both humans and cattle become secure; then, when he sacrifices with the morning offerings (*iṣṭis*), he truly seeks him [the lost object], and therefore one goes about seeking what was lost during the day. Furthermore, when he offers the *dhṛti* oblations in the evening and sacrifices with the morning *iṣṭis*, the sacrificer thereby provides for his acquisition and security (*yogakṣema*). Therefore, wherever they sacrifice with this sacrifice, it is provided for.

The security and prosperity of the subjects are secured. 13.1.5. [1] Indeed, prosperity and the kingdom depart from him who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice. For when a man attains prosperity, the lute is played for him; two Brāhmaṇas, lute-players and singers, sing for a year for the sake of prosperity.
This is the form of the lute: it bestows beauty upon him.
Regarding this, they say: "If two Brāhmaṇas were to sing, the Kṣatra would depart from him;
for this is the form of the Brāhmaṇa, and the Kṣatra does not find rest in the Brāhmaṇa."

If two *rājanya*s were to sing [the *sāman*] for him, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) would depart from him; for the *rājanya* is the form of the *kṣatra*, and spiritual luster does not abide in the *kṣatra*. One sings as a Brāhmaṇa, the other as a *rājanya*;
the Brāhmaṇa is indeed the *brahman*, and the *rājanya* is the *kṣatra*. Thus, by means of both his *brahman* and his *kṣatra*...
Thus, prosperity (*śrī*) becomes embraced from both sides.
Regarding this they say: "If both were to sing by day, prosperity would be liable to fall away from him. Day is indeed the form of the Brahmin;
for when a king desires, he then overcomes the Brahmin, yet he becomes worse off."

"If both were to sing at night, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) would depart from him; for the night is the form of the *kṣatra*, and spiritual luster does not abide in the *kṣatra*. Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa sings by day and the Rājanya sings by night; thus his prosperity is encompassed on both sides, by both the *brahman* and the *kṣatra*. (13.1.5)

"He sacrificed," "He gave"—thus the Brāhmaṇa sings; for the Brāhmaṇa's [merit] consists of sacrifice and pious works (*iṣṭāpūrta*); by means of sacrifice and pious works he indeed causes him to prosper. "He fought," "He won that battle"—thus the Rājanya sings; for the Rājanya's [merit] consists of battle and heroism (*vīrya*); by means of battle and heroism he indeed causes him to prosper. One sings three *gāthās*, the other sings three.
They amount to six; there are six seasons in the year. He thus finds firm support in the seasons, in the year. To those two he gives a hundred;
for man has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundred powers. Verily, he bestows life, power, and vigor upon himself.
"Vast through thy mother, abundant through thy father"—this earth is indeed the mother and yonder sky is the father; verily, he entrusts him to these two. "Thou art a horse."
With "Thou art a horse," he indeed instructs him; therefore, vigorous offspring are born. With "Thou art a steed, thou art a joy," he leads him forward;

therefore, the horse attains preeminence among animals. With "Thou art a racer, thou art a courser, thou art a prize-winner," it is according to the sacrificial formula. With "Thou art a bull, thou art manly-minded," it is for the sake of pairing. "Thy name is Yavya, thy name is Śiśu"—this indeed [is so].
The horse’s dear name; he addresses it by its very dear name. Therefore, even when two enemies meet and address each other by name, they recognize one another as friends.
"Go along the path of the Ādityas," he says; he thus causes it to go to the Ādityas themselves. "O guardians of the quarters, bring this horse to the gods."
"Protect that which has been sprinkled for wisdom!"—there are indeed one hundred princes of the bedchamber who are guardians of the quarters; it is to them that he entrusts him.

"May there be delight here, may there be pleasure here, may there be steadfastness here, may there be self-steadfastness, Svāhā!"—for a year he offers these oblations, sixteen nineties; these indeed are the fetters of the horse, and by means of them he [binds] him.

Therefore, even when released, the horse returns to its tether. There are sixteen times ninety of these [repetitions]; by means of them he binds it. Therefore, even when released, the horse does not abandon its tether. 13.1.6. [3] The Aśvamedha is indeed the kingdom. Those who guard the horse strive for the kingdom; of them, whoever reaches the end...
Those who reach the ultimate goal go to the kingdom itself and become part of the kingdom; but those who do not reach the ultimate goal are cut off from the kingdom.

Therefore, one who possesses a kingdom should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha. Indeed, he who, being weak, sacrifices with the Aśvamedha is cast away. If enemies should capture his horse, his sacrifice would be cut asunder.

If one who is worse [than the victim] should be sought, they protect him by wearing armor for the sake of the continuity of the sacrifice and to prevent its interruption; thus he does not become worse. Then, having brought another, they should sprinkle him; that indeed is the expiation in that case.
Prajāpati desired, "May I sacrifice with the Aśvamedha. He exerted himself and practiced austerity. Of him, thus exhausted...

When he was heated, the deities departed from him who consists of seven elements; that became the *dīkṣā*. He saw these *vaiśvadeva* offerings; he offered them, and by means of them he obtained the *dīkṣā*.
In that he offers the *vaiśvadeva* oblations, the sacrificer thereby obtains the *dīkṣā*. He offers them day after day; verily, day after day he obtains the *dīkṣā*.

He offers seven oblations; for those seven deities indeed departed, and through them he secures initiation for him. Indeed, the vital breaths depart from those who prolong the initiation beyond its proper time. They perform the rite for seven days; for there are seven vital breaths in the head, and initiation is the vital breaths; thus, by means of the vital breaths, he secures the vital breaths and initiation for him. It is threefold.

Having divided [the oblation], he offers it to the deity. The gods are indeed threefold, and these worlds are threefold; thus, through prosperity and vigor, he becomes firmly established in these worlds.
They amount to twenty-one: twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun.
The twenty-first is that divinity, that is the ruling power (*kṣatra*), that is prosperity (*śrī*), that is sovereignty; he enjoys that world of the Sun (*bradhna*) and that self-rule (*svārājya*).
He offers thirty *audgrabhaṇa* oblations; the Virāj consists of thirty syllables, and the Virāj is indeed all food.

He offers four *audgrabhaṇa* oblations for the attainment of all food. Three are dedicated to the Viśvedevas; they amount to seven. There are indeed seven vital breaths in the head. By means of the vital breaths, he secures the consecration (*dīkṣā*) and the vital breaths for him. He offers the final *pūrṇāhuti* for support and for union. 13.1.8 [1]
Prajāpati created the Aśvamedha; once created, it collapsed forward in its Ṛc and collapsed backward in its Sāman.
The Vaiśvadeva offerings supported it. In that he offers the Vaiśvadeva oblations, it is for the sake of supporting the Aśvamedha itself.
"To Kāya svāhā! To Ka-smai svāhā! To Katamas-mai svāhā!"—thus he makes the offering to Prajāpati the principal one.
Verily, he raises him up with those deities who have Prajāpati as their mouth.
"Svāhā to the resolve, to the resolved; svāhā to the mind, to Prajāpati; svāhā to the thought, to the knower"—whatever the Brāhmaṇa explanation was for the former [oblations], that is the same here.
"Aditi, svāhā! Aditi the Great, svāhā! Aditi the Very Gracious, svāhā!"—for Aditi is this [earth]; verily with her he raises him up.
"Sarasvatī, svāhā! Sarasvatī the Purifying, svāhā! Sarasvatī the Vast, svāhā!"—for Sarasvatī is speech.
By means of speech itself, Sarasvatī raises him up.
"To Pūṣan, svāhā! To Pūṣan, the protector of paths, svāhā! To Pūṣan, the bestower of wealth, svāhā!"—Pūṣan is indeed cattle;
by means of cattle, he raises him up.

"To Tvaṣṭṛ, svāhā! To Tvaṣṭṛ the drop-maker, svāhā! To Tvaṣṭṛ of many forms, svāhā! Tvaṣṭṛ is indeed the fashioner of the forms of paired animals; verily, by means of their forms, he raises him up. "To Viṣṇu, svāhā! To Viṣṇu the protector of the secret, svāhā! To Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa, svāhā! The sacrifice, indeed, is Viṣṇu.

"Viṣṇu indeed raises him up by means of the sacrifice. With the verse, "Of every god who leads," he offers the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). This earth is indeed the full oblation; thus, in the end, he finds firm support upon this very earth. "O Brahman, may a Brāhmaṇa be born endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*). Thus, spiritual luster is produced specifically in the Brāhmaṇa.

He bestows it; therefore, in former times, a Brāhmaṇa was born endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*). [13.1.9.2] "May a Kṣatriya be born in the kingdom—one who is a hero, skilled in archery, a piercer of the mark, and a great chariot-warrior. Thus he bestows heroism and greatness upon the Kṣatriya himself; therefore, in former times, a Kṣatriya was born who was a hero, skilled in archery, a piercer of the mark, and a great chariot-warrior. [13.1.9.3]
"Milking is the cow"—he thus places milk in the cow; therefore, in former times, the cow was born as one that milks.
"A burden-bearer is the ox"—he thus places strength in the ox; therefore, in former times, the ox was born as a burden-bearer.
"Swift is the steed"—he thus places speed in the horse; therefore, in former times, the horse was born as a runner.

"Of whom Puraṃdhi is the wife"—this form he bestows upon the woman alone; therefore, a beautiful young woman is beloved. 13.1.9.[7] "The victorious one standing on the chariot"—this the Rājanya alone bestows as his victorious majesty; therefore, in former times, the Rājanya was born as a conqueror. 13.1.9.[8]
"May he be a youth fit for the assembly"—he who is in his first youth is indeed fit for the assembly; therefore, one in his first youth is likely to be dear to women.
"May a hero be born to this sacrificer"—this places heroic power in the progeny of the sacrificer himself.
Therefore, from that which was previously born, Vīra was born.

"May Parjanya rain for us according to our desire"—for wherever they sacrifice with this sacrifice, Parjanya rains according to their every desire. "May our plants ripen fruitfully"—for indeed, they do ripen fruitfully.

There the medicinal herbs ripen where they sacrifice with this sacrifice, [thinking], "May our acquisition and security be provided for. Indeed, acquisition and security are provided for there where they sacrifice with this sacrifice; therefore, wherever they sacrifice with this sacrifice, the acquisition and security of the people becomes established. 13.2.1. [1]

Prajāpati assigned the sacrifices to the gods; he kept the Aśvamedha for himself. Those gods said to Prajāpati, "The Aśvamedha is indeed the sacrifice; let there be a share for us here as well. For them, he prepared these food-oblations (*annahoma*). In that he offers the food-oblations, he thereby gratifies the gods. 13.2.1 [2]

He offers with clarified butter (ājya). Clarified butter is indeed splendor; verily, by means of splendor he bestows splendor upon him. He offers with clarified butter; for clarified butter is the beloved abode of the gods; verily, he prospers them with their own beloved abode. (13.2.1.3) He offers with parched groats (saktu). Parched groats are indeed the form of the gods; verily, he thus gratifies the gods. (13.2.1.4)

He offers with parched grains (*dhānā*). Parched grains are indeed the form of days and nights; thus he gratifies the days and nights. He offers with fried grains (*lāja*). Fried grains are indeed the form of the constellations (*nakṣatra*); thus he gratifies the constellations. "To breath, svāhā! To out-breath, svāhā!"—thus he offers while pronouncing their names; by pronouncing their names, he gratifies them. "To the One, svāhā!"
With "Svāhā to two! Svāhā to a hundred! Svāhā to one hundred and one! he offers in regular succession;
thus he gratifies them in their proper order. He offers with increments of one; for the heavenly world is single-stepped (unitary);
verily, he causes him to go to the heavenly world in a single direction. He offers consecutively; for the heavenly world is, as it were, turned away.
For the conquest of the heavenly world. Indeed, he who offers oblations directed away is liable to be burnt up. He does not exceed one hundred and one;
for were he to exceed one hundred and one, he would deprive the sacrificer of his life. He offers one hundred and one; for man has a lifespan of a hundred years.
With "To the Self, hail! To the One-Hundred-and-One-fold Life-span, hail! To the Self, hail! he establishes himself within his own life-span. With "To the Dawn, hail! To Heaven, hail!

he offers the two final oblations. Night indeed is the Dawn; Day is Heaven. Thus he gratifies both day and night. Regarding this they say: "If one were to offer both [oblations] either by day or by night, he would confuse day and night; [therefore, one should offer them at dawn] for the sake of the Dawn."
He offers with "Svāhā! before the sun has risen; with "Svāhā to heaven! once it has risen, so that there may be no confusion between day and night.
(13.2.2.1) The Aśvamedha is indeed the king of sacrifices. When the sacrificer undertakes the horse-sacrifice, he becomes the horse, the sacrificer becomes the sacrifice.
When he binds the sacrificial animals to the horse, he places them within the sacrifice itself. (13.2.2.2)

He immolates a horse, a hornless goat, and a gayal at the central sacrificial post; by this, he sharpens the vanguard of his army, and therefore the vanguard of a king becomes formidable. He offers a black-necked animal sacred to Agni on the forehead in front; he thereby establishes the eastern fire, and therefore [the king's]—
The eastern fire is destined to be prosperous.
[13.2.2.4] He offers a ewe to Sarasvatī below the two shoulder-blades; thereby he makes women followers of men; therefore women are destined to be followers of men.
Two goats with dark lower parts for the Aśvins are offered at the two forelegs; verily he bestows strength upon the two forelegs, and therefore a king is destined to possess strength of arm.
[13.2.2.6] A dark animal for Soma and Pūṣan is offered at the navel; verily he establishes that foundation, for Pūṣan is this earth, and thus he finds support upon her.
The two [amulets] for Sūrya and Yama, white and black respectively, he places on the two sides as armor; therefore, a king, when armored, displays his prowess.
The two belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ, with hairy thighs, he places on the two thighs; he thus bestows strength upon the thighs; therefore, a king is destined to possess strong thighs.

A white animal for Vāyu at the tail; he thereby creates a swelling, and therefore offspring resort to a swelling in times of fear. A cow that miscarries for Indra Svapasya, for the sake of the sacrifice’s possession of Indra.
A dwarf for Viṣṇu; Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; thus in the end, he finds firm support in the sacrifice itself. 13.2.2 [10]
These fifteen animals are indeed those bound to the horse; for the thunderbolt is fifteenfold, and the thunderbolt is vigor.
By means of that very thunderbolt, by means of that vigor, the sacrificer repels evil from the front.
There are fifteen in each of the others as well; for the thunderbolt is fifteenfold, and the thunderbolt is vigor.
By this very thunderbolt, by this very vigor, the sacrificer drives away evil on all sides.
Regarding this, they say: "Surely one has driven away evil with these [offerings]," yet he restores Prajāpati only incompletely and does not obtain this entire universe.
One should immolate seventeen animals at the central sacrificial post; for Prajāpati is seventeenfold, and the Aśvamedha is Prajāpati.
This is for the attainment of the Aśvamedha itself. There are sixteen on each of the other posts; for this entire world consists of sixteen parts, and thus he secures this entire world. 13.2.2. [14]

"How should one satisfy them? they asked. "With the verses beginning 'The kindled [fire], anointing, the fulfiller of prayers'—one should satisfy them with the Bārhadukthī verses. For Bṛhaduktha Vāmadevya, or Aśva Sāmudri, saw these *āprī* verses for the horse; saying, "These are they; with these very verses we shall now satisfy him," they do not proceed in that manner.
One should perform the *aprī* verses with those belonging to Jamadagni. Jamadagni is indeed Prajāpati, and he is the Aśvamedha;
thus he endows it with its own deity. Therefore, one should perform the *aprī* verses with those belonging to Jamadagni.
Regarding this, some make separate *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses for these animals tied to the horse's limbs (*paryaṅgya*), [thinking] "we shall find..."

Thinking, "We will not perform [the rites] for these others because we have not obtained these," one should not do so. For the horse is the nobility (*kṣatra*), and the other animals are the peasantry (*viś*).

Those who act thus make the peasantry a counterweight and an adversary to the nobility; moreover, they deprive the sacrificer of his life-span. Therefore, the horse belongs to Prajāpati, while the others belong to the gods.
Verily, he makes the people subject to the kṣatriya as one who follows his path; moreover, he prospers the sacrificer through long life. 13.2.2 [16]
The horse's goad is made of gold, those for the animals tied to the horse (paryaṅgyas) are made of copper, and those for the others are made of iron.

Gold is indeed light, and the Aśvamedha is sovereignty; thus he bestows light upon the kingdom. Moreover, by means of the light that is gold, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world; furthermore, he thereby makes it a mirror for the heavenly world.

For the sake of unification. Furthermore, the horse is indeed the ruling power (*kṣatra*); gold is the form of the ruling power; thus he causes the ruling power to prosper by means of the ruling power.

Now, as to why they are made of copper for those animals tied to the horse's limbs: just as the king’s royal servants, the charioteers and the village headmen, are subordinate to the king, so indeed are these animals tied to the limbs subordinate to the horse; and just as copper is a form of gold, he thus endows them with their own proper form. 13.2.2. [19]
Now, as for the fact that the others [the limbs] are made of iron: the other animals are the people (*viś*), and iron is the form of the people; thus he unites the people with the people.

They cut portions of the horse on the north side in a basket of cane-wood; for the horse is connected to the *anuṣṭubh*, and this direction (the north) is connected to the *anuṣṭubh*; thus he places it in its own quarter. And as for the basket of cane-wood: [the horse] has its origin in the waters.
The horse is born of the waters; the reed (*vetasa*) is born of the waters. Thus, he causes it to prosper by means of its own womb. 13.2.3.

The gods, indeed, did not know the path to the heavenly world during the Aśvamedha; the horse knew it. Therefore, when they glide along with the horse for the sake of the Pavamāna [Soma] in the Aśvamedha, it is for the purpose of knowing the heavenly world.

They touch the tail [of the horse] for the attainment of the heavenly world; for a human does not know the heavenly world directly, but the horse indeed knows the heavenly world directly. (13.2.3) If the Udgātṛ were to sing the chant, it would be as if one who does not know the terrain were to lead by another path; such would that be.
In that he chooses the horse for the *udgītha* after having secured the *udgātṛ*, it is just as one who knows the way leads directly;
even so, the horse leads the sacrificer directly to the heavenly world. He utters the *hiṅ* sound; he utters the *hiṅ* sound for the sake of the *sāman*;
he is indeed the *udgītha*. They tether the mares and they neigh together, just like the accompanying singers.

They sing around it; such is that gold, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the gold weighing one hundred measures (*śatamāna*). Its *brāhmaṇa* has been explained. Prajāpati desired, "May I conquer both worlds: the world of the gods and the world of men.
He saw these domestic animals and immolated them; by means of them, he won these two worlds, indeed by means of the domestic ones.

By means of domestic animals he won this world, and by means of wild animals that [other] world. This world is indeed the world of men, while that is the world of the gods. In that he sacrifices domestic animals, the sacrificer wins this very world by them; in that he sacrifices wild animals, he wins that [world] by them. 13.2.4. [2]
If he were to establish it with village animals, the roads would become congested, the boundaries of two villages would be contiguous, and *ṛkṣīkas*, "man-tigers," robbers, murderers,
and thieves would be born in the forests. If he were to establish it with wild animals, the roads would be desolate and distant.

The boundaries of two villages would be [in conflict], and Ṛkṣīkas, tigers among men, plunderers, archers, and thieves would be born in the forests. Regarding this they say: "That which is wild is indeed without cattle; one should not offer an oblation to it. If one were to offer, [misfortune would come] quickly."

If they were to carry the deceased sacrificer to the forest, [it would be wrong], for wild animals have their portion in the forest; if one were not to offer them, it would be a desecration of the sacrifice. Therefore, they release them after the fire has been carried around them (*paryagnikṛta*); thus it is neither offered nor unoffered.
They do not carry the deceased sacrificer to the forest, and there is no desecration of the sacrifice. 13.2.4. [4]
He establishes [the boundary] with village-dwellers; thus father and son reach an agreement and travel together on the road.
The borders of two villages become contiguous; there are no *ṛkṣīkas*, man-tigers, robbers, murderers, or thieves born in the forests. 13.2.5.[1]

Prajāpati created the Aśvamedha. Once created, it went away from him; having become a *paṅkti*, it entered the year. It became the half-months. He employed it with the fifteenfold [stomas] and attained it. Having attained it, he secured it by means of the fifteenfold [stomas]. This fifteenfold [stoma] is indeed the image of the half-months.
In that he offers animals with fifteen parts, the sacrificer thereby secures the half-months.
Regarding this they say: "The year indeed remains unsecured for him who performs the year-long rite other than through the Cāturmāsya sacrifices. For the Cāturmāsyas are truly the manifest year.

In that he immolates the animals of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, he directly wins the year. He who extends the year apart from the sets of eleven animals is indeed deprived of progeny and cattle and fails to reach the heavenly world. This set of eleven animals is truly the heavenly world itself; for the set of eleven is indeed progeny and cattle.

When one sacrifices the eleven animals, he does not miss the heavenly world, nor is he deprived of offspring and cattle. Prajāpati created the Virāj; once she was created from him, she turned away and entered the sacrificial horse. 13.2.5 [3] He [Prajāpati] [pursued her].
He offered it with ten-syllable [verses]; he obtained it; having obtained it, he secured it by means of the ten-syllable [verses].
In that he offers animals with ten-syllable [verses], the sacrificer secures the Virāj itself by them. He offers a hundred; man indeed has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred powers;
verily, he places life, power, and vigor within himself. 13.2.5 [4]

He sacrifices eleven sets of ten; for the *triṣṭubh* consists of eleven syllables, and the *triṣṭubh* is indeed power and vigor; it is for the attainment of power and vigor that he sacrifices eleven sets of ten. There are ten vital breaths in an animal, and the self is the eleventh; thus, by means of the vital breaths, he makes the animals prosper. They belong to the Viśvedevas, for [the sacrifice] belongs to the Viśvedevas.

The horse becomes many-formed for the sake of the horse's wholeness; therefore cattle are many-formed, therefore cattle are of various forms. "They yoke the ruddy, bright one as he moves"—the ruddy, bright one is indeed yonder sun; it is yonder sun that they yoke for him. 13.2.6 [1]
He yokes the sun for the attainment of the heavenly world.
Regarding this, they say: "The sacrifice indeed turns away from him whose sacrificial animal, once dedicated, goes elsewhere than to the altar. [The sacrificer says:
"O singer, by this path bring the horse back again! Vāyu is indeed the singer; it is him he brings back to him.
He places this at the end so that it does not pass beyond.
From him who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice, brilliance, sensory power, cattle, and prosperity depart.
"May the Vasus anoint you with the Gāyatrī metre," [with these words] the queen anoints [the horse]; for ghee is brilliance and the Gāyatrī is brilliance.
Verily, he places two concordant [powers] within this very brilliance.

(13.2.6.5) "May the Rudras anoint you with the Triṣṭubh metre!"—the ghee is indeed brilliance, and the Triṣṭubh is power; verily, he places both brilliance and power within him as two concordant [powers]. (13.2.6.6)
"May the Ādityas anoint you with the Jagatī metre! he says. Clarified butter is indeed brilliance, and the Jagatī is cattle;
thus he bestows both brilliance and cattle upon him in a unified manner.
The wives anoint [him]; for the wives are the form of prosperity (*śrī*); it is prosperity itself that they bestow upon him.
From him neither brilliance, nor the senses, nor cattle, nor fortune depart.
(13.2.6.8) Just as the oblation might spill before it is offered, so does this [sacrifice] spill for one whose hair falls out while he is being washed.
When they grind glass beads, they thereby collect his very hair. They are made of gold; regarding that, it has already been explained.
They cause one hundred and one Brahmins to weave [the cloth] with a single thread; man has a lifespan of a hundred years and the self is the one hundred and first;

thus he establishes himself in his own life-span and self. With the formulas "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," they weave it with the verses addressed to Prajāpati; the horse belongs to Prajāpati; they thus endow it with its own deity.
"O you who scatter the parched grain, O you who sing, O you who weave, O you who weave wool! [Thus they say.]

Thus he brings down this extra food for the horse; he thereby makes the offspring eaters of food. "Eat this food, O gods; eat this food, O Prajāpati"—he thus causes the offspring to prosper through the eating of food. 13.2.6.
[9] Indeed, brilliance and sacred luster depart from him who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice—the Hotṛ and the Brahman.
And as they engage in the theological debate (*brahmodya*), [it is said]: "The Hotṛ is indeed connected with Agni, and the Brahman is connected with Bṛhaspati;

Bṛhaspati is the *brahman*. Thus, they bestow upon him both splendor and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) in a unified manner. As they speak on both sides of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), [it is understood that] the post is indeed the sacrificer; thus, they place the sacrificer himself on both sides with splendor and spiritual luster.
“They put on [the garment]. “Who indeed wanders alone? “Yonder sun indeed wanders alone; he is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
Thus they bestow spiritual luster upon him.”

"Who indeed is born again? The moon, indeed, is born again; they thus bestow life-span upon him. "What is the remedy for cold? Fire, indeed, is the remedy for cold; they thus bestow radiance upon him. "What is the great receptacle? This world, indeed, is the great receptacle; [they bestow it] in this very world.
He establishes himself. (13.2.6.14) "What was the first thought? Heaven, indeed, is the first thought; verily, he wins heaven and rain.
(13.2.6.15) "What was the great bird? The horse, indeed, is the great bird; verily, he wins life. (13.2.6.16)

"Who was it that was *pilippilā*? "Fortune (*śrī*) indeed is *pilippilā*. [Thus he] secures fortune for himself. "Who was it that was *piśaṅgilā*? "Day and night indeed are *piśaṅgilā*. [Thus he] becomes firmly established in day and night.
When the animals have been assigned, the Adhvaryu takes up the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*), while the sacrificer maintains contact with him as he is about to sprinkle the horse.
The sacrificer, having recited the formula pertaining to the *ādhvara* sacrifice, proceeds to the formula pertaining to the *aśvamedha*:
"May Vāyu protect thee with cooked offerings"—Vāyu indeed cooks him; "and may Agni, the black-necked, [protect thee] with goats"—Agni, indeed, is the black-necked;
Agni himself cooks him with goats. 13.2.7. [2-3]
"The banyan tree with the cups"—where the gods indeed sacrificed with the sacrifice, they turned these cups downward;
therefore, the banyan trees grow facing downward.
"The silk-cotton tree with prosperity"—he bestows prosperity upon the silk-cotton tree; therefore, the silk-cotton tree is the tallest among the lords of the forest.

With the words "This stallion, fit for the chariot," he equips the chariot with the horse; therefore, the horse does not draw anything other than the chariot (13.2.7.6). "With six, with four, he has come hither"—therefore, when standing still, the horse stands on three legs, but when yoked, it stands on all four.
"May Brahmākṛṣṇa protect us with his six [feet]"—Brahmākṛṣṇa is indeed the moon; he thus entrusts him to the moon.
"Homage to Agni"—he thus pays homage to Agni. 13.2.7.[8]

"Sharpened by the rein is the chariot"—thus he perfects the chariot with the rein; therefore the chariot, when harnessed, becomes most beautiful to behold. "Sharpened by the rein is the horse"—thus he perfects the horse with the rein; therefore the horse is guided by the rein.

"It is most pleasing" (bhūyiṣṭhaṃ rocate). "Sharpened in the waters, born of the waters"—for the horse has its origin in the waters; thus he endows it with its own womb. "The Brahman, with Soma as his leader"—thus he causes it to go to the heavenly world with Soma as its leader.
"Fashion your own body for yourself"—by this he says to him, "Assume whatever form you desire";

"Sacrifice yourself"—he thereby bestows self-sovereignty upon him; "Enjoy yourself"—by this he says to him, "Make your own world shine as far as you desire"; "No other can attain your greatness"—[this refers] to the horse itself.
"By his greatness he prospers.

(13.2.7.12) "Truly, you do not die here, nor do you suffer harm"—this he thus comforts him. "Thou goest indeed to the gods by easy paths"—he thus shows him the very paths traveled by the gods, [saying], "where the doers of good deeds abide, where they have gone."

He makes him share the same world as those who have performed good deeds. With the words, "May the god Savitṛ place you there," Savitṛ himself places him in the heavenly world. With the words, "I sprinkle you, acceptable to Prajāpati," he murmurs softly; then he takes hold [of the vessel]. Agni was the sacrificial animal; with it they sacrificed, and he won this world in which Agni dwells. That shall be your world.

"You shall conquer him; drink these waters!"—by this he says to him: "As great as is Agni’s victory, as great as is his world, and as great as is his sovereignty, so great shall be your victory, so great your world, and so great your sovereignty.
Vāyu was the sacrificial animal; they sacrificed with it, and he conquered that world in which Vāyu dwells. That world shall be yours.
"You shall conquer that; drink these waters!"—as great as is the victory of Vāyu, as great as is his world.

Sūrya was the sacrificial animal; with him they sacrificed, and he conquered this world in which Sūrya dwells. That world shall be yours; you shall conquer it; drink these waters! As great as is the victory of Sūrya, as great as is his world, as great as is his sovereignty—so great shall yours be.

"Victory shall be yours, such a world shall be yours, and such sovereignty shall be yours"—this is what he says to him at that time. Having gratified the horse and consecrated it again, he sprinkles the other animals with the *prokṣaṇī* waters. Regarding this, [the text says]:
"The gods, indeed, did not know the way to the heavenly world; the horse knew it. Therefore, they proceed toward the north with the horse. (13.2.8)

For the sake of making known the heavenly world, they spread out for the horse a cloth, an upper garment, and gold, as one does not do for any other animal; upon that they quiet it, thereby distinguishing it from other animals. 13.2.8 [2]

They indeed kill this animal when they quiet it. While it is being quieted, he offers oblations with the words, "To out-breathing, svāhā! To in-breathing, svāhā! To diffused breathing, svāhā! He thereby places the vital breaths into it; thus, his sacrifice is performed with the animal as if it were still alive. 13.2.8 [3]
"O Amba, O Ambika, O Ambalika, let no one lead me away"—with these words he leads his wives forward; he thus calls them, and furthermore, he makes them pure for the sacrifice.
"We invoke thee, the lord of hosts among hosts"—with these words the wives walk around him; he thereby denies him [the company of others]. 13.2.8. [4]
They indeed deny him nothing, and they also establish him. They go around him three times;

for these worlds are three, and it is by means of these worlds that they establish him. They go around him three times again, making six in total; for there are six seasons, and it is by means of the seasons that they establish him. 13.2.8 [5]
The vital breaths indeed depart from those who perform the shaking at the sacrifice. They go around nine times;

for there are nine vital breaths. Thus they place the vital breaths within themselves, so that the vital breaths do not depart from them. With the words, "I have brought forth the one who bears the embryo; you have brought forth the one who bears the embryo,"—for embryos are indeed offspring and cattle—they thereby secure offspring.

He bestows the animals upon himself. "May you two both stretch out your four feet," he says, for the sake of securing a pair. "In the heavenly world, may you two cover yourselves," he says; for that indeed is the heavenly world where they immolate the animal. Therefore he speaks thus: "May the vigorous stallion, the depositor of seed, deposit seed," for the sake of securing a pair. 13.2.9. [1]

Prosperity and the kingdom depart from him who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice. "Raise her up," he says; for the Aśvamedha is prosperity and the kingdom. Verily, he raises prosperity and the kingdom upward for him.

"Like one carrying a burden on a mountain"—for the royal power (*śrī*) is indeed the burden of the kingdom; he thus equips him with royal power, and moreover, he places royal power upon him within the kingdom. "And may her middle prosper"—for the royal power is indeed the middle of the kingdom; [he thus places] royal power in the kingdom.
In the middle he places food to eat. [13.2.9.5] "As if purifying in a cold wind," he says; the cold is indeed security for the kingdom; verily, he provides security for him.
[13.2.9.6] "The little bird, yakāsaka," he says; the little bird is the people (*viś*); "it flutters with a *ahalak* sound," he says; the people are indeed for the sake of the kingdom.
"Deceiving, they strike at the womb; the fetter rings out, 'O guardian! The people (*viś*) are indeed the womb, and the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*) is the fetter.
He thus strikes the kingdom against the people; therefore, the ruler is one who slays the people.
"Both your mother and your father"—this earth is indeed the mother and yonder sky is the father. By means of these two, he [leads him] to the heavenly world.

"He makes him reach the top of the tree; it grows. Prosperity (*śrī*) is indeed the top of the kingdom; verily, he causes him to reach prosperity, the top of the kingdom. "'The grasping one,' so [says the verse]; 'in the womb his father loosened his fist. The people (*viś*) are indeed the womb, and the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*) is the fist; he strikes the kingdom into the people. Therefore, the ruler of the kingdom is a slayer of the people. (13.2.9)
Because it is said, "The *hariṇa* eats barley," barley is indeed the peasantry (*viś*) and the *hariṇa* is the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*); thus he makes the peasantry edible for the kingdom.
Therefore, the kingdom eats the peasantry; [as it is said], "He does not consider the cattle to be nourished," therefore the king does not rear cattle.
[As it is said], "A *śūdrā* who has a noble lover is neither for nourishment nor for wealth," therefore one does not consecrate the son of a *vaiśī*. 13.2.9. [9]
The vital breaths indeed depart from those who speak impure speech at the sacrifice.

Therefore, they recite at the end the verse containing the word "surabhi" (fragrant), namely, "I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan. Thus they purify their speech; the vital breaths do not depart from them. 13.2.10.1.
When they fashion the sword-paths, the sacrificer makes that very bridge and crossing for the attainment of the heavenly world.
They fashion [the altar] with needles; the needles are the subjects (*viś*), and the Aśvamedha is the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*); thus he bestows both the subjects and the kingdom upon him.
They place the *samīcī* bricks; they are made of gold; the Brāhmaṇa concerning them has been explained.

There are three kinds of needles: those made of copper, those of silver, and those of *hariṇī* (yellow) metal. The quarters are indeed represented by the copper ones, the intermediate quarters by the silver ones, and the upward directions by the *hariṇī* ones. With these—both the horizontal and the vertical—they fashion it in many forms.
Therefore the quarters are of many forms; therefore the quarters are of various forms.

13.2.11 [1] Prajāpati desired, "May I become great and more abundant. He saw these two *mahiman* cups at the Aśvamedha sacrifice; he offered them, and thereby he indeed became great and more abundant. He who should desire...
Thinking, "May I become great and more abundant," he should offer these two *mahiman* cups in the *Aśvamedha*; indeed, he becomes great and more abundant.
He offers [the *mahiman* cups] on both sides of the omentum; for the *Aśvamedha* is the sacrificer, and the *mahiman* is the king; thus, by means of kingship itself, he encompasses him on both sides.

He takes hold [of it] from the front; for some gods have their *svāhā*-utterances before, while others have their *svāhā*-utterances after—it is these very ones he thus gratifies with the words, "Svāhā to the gods! To the gods, svāhā! With the King [Soma], he completely encompasses the omentum;
thus he gratifies both the gods who are in this world and those who are in yonder world. These gods, being gratified, [favor him].

They carry one to the heavenly world. 13.3.1.[1] The eye of Prajāpati swelled; it fell away, and from that the horse (*aśva*) came into being. Because it swelled (*aśvayat*), that is the "horseness" (*aśvatva*) of the horse. The gods restored it by means of the Aśvamedha sacrifice itself. This...
Verily, he who sacrifices with the Aśvamedha makes Prajāpati whole; he himself becomes everything.

This is indeed the expiation for everything, the remedy for everything. By means of this, the gods overcame all evil, and they even overcame the murder of a Brahmin by it; he overcomes all evil and overcomes the murder of a Brahmin.

He who performs the horse sacrifice—13.3.1.[2] That [eye] of Prajāpati swelled upward; therefore, they cut portions from the horse on the left side, whereas for other animals, they cut from the right side. 13.3.1.[3]
The mat is made of reeds; for the horse has its origin in the waters, and the reed is born from the waters; he thus endows it with its own womb.
The Stoma is the Catuṣṭoma; for the Catuṣṭoma indeed tore open the two thighs of the horse, and the gods [repaired it] by means of the Catuṣṭoma itself.
They restored it by means of the *stoma*; in that the *catuṣṭoma* *stoma* occurs, it is for the sake of the horse’s completeness.

The final day is an *atirātra* with all the *stomas*; for the *atirātra* with all the *stomas* is everything, and the *Aśvamedha* is everything—for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything. 13.3.2. [1]
Having conquered by means of the supreme Stoma, the Catuṣṭoma, on the next day of the Ayana, he establishes himself upon the twenty-one-fold Stoma as a firm foundation.
From that twenty-one-fold foundation, he ascends on the following day to the Seasons; for the Pṛṣṭhas are indeed the Seasons, and the Seasons are the Year.
Thus, he establishes himself in the Seasons, in the Year. 13.3.2. [2]

The Śakvarī verses constitute the *pṛṣṭha* chant; here different meters are used and different animals are sacrificed—both domestic and wild, as it were. That the Śakvarīs form the *pṛṣṭha* is for the sake of the horse’s completeness. Other animals are sacrificed, for other and distinct *stomas* are performed. 13.3.2. [3]

Regarding this they say: "These are not all the animals—namely, goats, sheep, and wild animals—for these indeed are all the animals that belong to the cattle. Therefore, on the final day he immolates those belonging to the cattle; for these indeed are all the animals that belong to the cattle. Thus he immolates all the animals.
They belong to the Viśvedevas, for the horse belongs to the Viśvedevas; it is for the sake of the completeness of the horse. They are of many forms.

Therefore, animals are multiform and possess various forms; therefore, animals are of diverse shapes. Because there are three *anuṣṭubh* verses, the horse stands on three legs; because there are four *gāyatrī* verses, the horse runs away, planting all its feet. This indeed is the supreme meter.

Since the horse is the supreme among animals and the *anuṣṭubh* is the supreme among meters, and since the *catuṣṭoma* is the supreme among *stomas*, he causes it to reach supremacy by means of that which is supreme.
The *śakvarī* verses constitute the *pṛṣṭha*; for different meters are employed and different *stomas* are performed.
The *yājyā*s become the back of the horse for the sake of its wholeness.
The middle day is the twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśa*); yonder sun is indeed the twenty-one-fold, and he is the Aśvamedha.
By means of its own *stoma*, it establishes him in his own deity.
The Vāmadevya, the Sāman of Mitrāvaruṇa, is used; the Vāmadevya is indeed Prajāpati, and the horse belongs to Prajāpati;
thus he endows it with its own deity.
The Pārthuraśma is the Brahman-Sāman; for by means of a rein the horse is restrained, and the horse is capable of being unrestrained and uncontrolled.

It is established for one who is about to go to the furthest distance that the *Brahmasāman* becomes the *Pārthuraśma*, for the sake of the horse's support. The *Saṃkṛti* is the *Āvākasāman*; for this Aśvamedha is, as it were, a sacrifice whose ritual has fallen into ruin—what indeed [could there be] for it?

What is performed, or what is not, such that it becomes the *acāvāk-sāman* for the sake of the horse’s completeness? The final day is an *atirātra* with all the *stomas*; for the *atirātra* with all the *stomas* is everything, and the *Aśvamedha* is everything—for the attainment of everything and the securing of everything. 13.3.3. [7]

The fire-altar consists of twenty-one parts, the *stoma* is twenty-onefold, and there are twenty-one sacrificial posts (*yūpa*). Just as bulls or stallions might clash together, so do these *stomas* collide when they are twenty-onefold. If he were to cause them to clash, the sacrificer would meet with ruin and his sacrifice would be destroyed. 13.3.3 [8]

The fire-altar should be twelvefold and there should be eleven sacrificial posts. In that the fire-altar is twelvefold, the year has twelve months; he thus attains the year-long sacrifice. As for the fact that there are eleven sacrificial posts—this set of eleven is measured out as the Virāj; its eleventh [post] is her udder, and by means of it he milks her. 13.3.3. [9]

Regarding this they say: "If there were twelve fires and eleven stakes, it would be as if one were to travel with a single-yoked cart; such would that be. Therefore, the fire-altar consists of twenty-one parts, the Stoma is twenty-onefold, and there are twenty-one stakes; thus, it is as if one were to travel with side-horses. This twenty-onefold [altar] is indeed the head of the sacrifice. He who knows the three heads in the Aśvamedha—verily, he becomes the head.
The fire-altar of kings consists of twenty-one parts; the *stoma* is twenty-onefold; there are twenty-one sacrificial posts.

These, indeed, are the three heads in the Aśvamedha. He who knows this becomes the head of kings. Or, he who knows the three humps in the Aśvamedha becomes the hump of kings. The fire-altar is twenty-onefold; the *stoma* is twenty-onefold.
There are twenty-one sacrificial posts in the Aśvamedha; these are the three humps. He who knows this becomes a hump among kings.
(13.3.4) Indeed, the horse is offered to all the deities. If one were to make it belong to Prajāpati alone, those deities who have no share would [be excluded].

With the words "May he deprive the eater of his portion" and "The *avakā* plant with its teeth, the roots of the teeth," he makes portions of clarified butter (*ājya*) and offers oblations to the deities while excluding [the *avakā*]. He thus satisfies with their respective portions those very deities who have no shares.
Having offered the *araṇye'nūcya* formulas, he offers the final oblation to Heaven and Earth.

All the deities are indeed established in heaven and earth; it is them he thus gratifies. The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict. They said, "O Agnis Sviṣṭakṛts, let us take for ourselves a special portion (uddhāra) of the horse;
with that we shall overcome the Asuras. They took the blood as their portion for the sake of overcoming their rivals.
In that he offers blood to the *Sviṣṭakṛt* deities, it serves for the overcoming of his rivals; by himself he prospers, and his hateful rival is defeated—he who knows thus.
He offers the first oblation with the neck of a *gomṛga*; the *gomṛgas* are indeed cattle, and Rudra is [the lord of] cattle.
By means of the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, he interposes the animals from Rudra; therefore, wherever this oblation of the Aśvamedha is offered, there Rudra does not harm the animals.
He offers the second oblation with a horse's hoof; for one-hoofed animals are indeed cattle, and Rudra is the Sviṣṭakṛt—the protector of the cattle.
With an iron ladle he offers the third oblation. For Rudra Sviṣṭakṛt is indeed made of iron; thus he interposes the offspring from Rudra.
Therefore, wherever this oblation of the Aśvamedha is offered, there Rudra does not harm the offspring. 13.3.5.[1]
In all worlds indeed, deaths are inherent. If one were not to offer oblations to them, death would find him in every world.

Since he offers oblations to the deaths, he conquers death in every world. Regarding this they say: "If, while offering, one were to look about much, saying, 'Svāhā to such-and-such! Svāhā to such-and-such! [what would happen?]"

"One should make death one's enemy; one should confine oneself within death. Thus, saying "Svāhā to Death," he offers a single oblation to a single [deity]. For indeed, there is only one death in yonder world, namely hunger;
it is that very one which he conquers in yonder world. 13.3.5. [3]
With the words, "Svāhā to the slaying of a Brahmin," he offers the second oblation. Indeed, there is another death that is not the slaying of a Brahmin;
this slaying of a Brahmin is truly death itself. Thus, he directly overcomes death. Muṇḍibha Audanya indeed discovered this expiation for the slaying of a Brahmin.

In that he offers the oblation for the slaying of a Brahmin, he satisfies Death itself with the oblation and provides protection; he thus prepares a remedy for the slayer of a Brahmin. Therefore, for whomever this oblation of the Aśvamedha is offered, even if he should kill a Brahmin among his other descendants, it provides a remedy for him. 13.3.6. [1]

When the horse was sacrificed, its vital essence (*medhas*) departed; that became the *Aśvastomīya*. In that he offers the *Aśvastomīya*, he endows the horse itself with its vital essence. He offers with clarified butter (*ājya*); clarified butter is indeed vital essence, and the *Aśvastomīya* is vital essence; thus, by means of vital essence, he bestows vital essence upon it.
He places [the oblation] and offers it with clarified butter (*ājya*). Clarified butter is indeed the dear abode of the gods; verily, he prospers them with their own dear abode.
Having offered the *Aśvastomīya*, he offers with two-footed verses; for the *Aśvastomīya* is the horse, and the two-footed verse is man.
Man indeed has two feet and is established on two; thus he endows him with a firm foundation.

Regarding this they say: "Should the *aśvastomīya* be offered first, or the *dvipadā*? The *aśvastomīya* is cattle, and man is the *dvipadā*. Since one offers the *dvipadā* after having offered the *aśvastomīya*, therefore man [is superior].
He stands over the animals from above.

He offers the sixteen *aśvastomīya* oblations; for animals consist of sixteen parts—that is the measure of animals. By this measure, he causes the animals to prosper. If he were to offer fewer or more than that, he would deprive the animals of their proper measure.

He offers sixteen oblations; for cattle consist of sixteen parts—that is the measure of cattle—and thus he causes cattle to prosper by means of their own measure. He does not offer any other final oblation; for if he were to offer another final oblation, he would fall away from his firm foundation. He offers a two-footed verse as the final one; for two-footed beings are a firm foundation, and thus he finds a firm foundation.

"Stand up for Jumbaka, svāhā!"—with these words he offers the final oblation at the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha). Jumbaka is indeed Varuṇa; thus he directly expiates Varuṇa. He offers it upon the head of a white, bald, moist-skinned, yellow-eyed dog;
for this is the form of Varuṇa. By means of his very form, he thus expiates Varuṇa. 13.3.6. [6]

Having risen, he offers twelve *brahmaudana* oblations and sacrifices with twelve *iṣṭis*. Regarding this, they say: "The *iṣṭis* are indeed the form of the sacrifice. If one were to sacrifice with the *iṣṭis*, the sacrifice would incline toward him, yet he would become worse off; for the meters of one who has already sacrificed become exhausted, so how could they be sufficient for such a short time?"
"One should employ [the speech] at all times; however, when the sacrifice has concluded, speech is obtained. Once obtained, it becomes exhausted and as if made harsh or wounded.
For speech is indeed the sacrifice; therefore, one should not employ it [at random].
"Having risen, he should offer twelve *brahmaudana* (sacrificial porridges for the Brahmins). The *odana* is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is..."
Prajāpati is the year; [he who performs this sacrifice] attains the year itself as the sacrifice. The sacrifice becomes inclined toward him, and he does not become worse off.
This sacrifice is indeed named "Abundant" (prabhū); wherever they perform this sacrifice, everything becomes abundant.

This is indeed the sacrifice named *Vibhū* (the Pervasive); when they sacrifice with this sacrifice, everything becomes pervaded. This is indeed the sacrifice named *Vyaṣṭi* (the Distinguished); when they sacrifice with this sacrifice, everything becomes distinguished.
This sacrifice is indeed called *vidhṛti*; when they sacrifice with this, everything becomes sustained.
This sacrifice is indeed called *vyāvṛtti*; when they sacrifice with this sacrifice, everything becomes distinguished.
This indeed is the sacrifice named "Full of Vitality" (*ūrjasvat*); when they sacrifice with this sacrifice, everything becomes full of vitality.
13.3.7.[7] This indeed is the sacrifice named "Full of Milk" (*payasvat*); when they sacrifice with this sacrifice, everything becomes full of milk.
13.3.7.[8] This indeed is the sacrifice named "Possessing Spiritual Splendor" (*brahmavarcasin*); when they sacrifice with this sacrifice, [the Brahmin]... 13.3.7.[9]

One is born endowed with the luster of Brahman. This sacrifice is indeed called "the piercer" (*ativyādhi*); when they perform this sacrifice, a Kṣatriya is born as a piercer. This sacrifice is indeed called "the long" (*dīrgha*); when they perform this sacrifice, a long forest is produced.
This sacrifice is indeed called *klpti*; when they sacrifice with this sacrifice, everything becomes arranged (*klpta*). 13.3.7.
[12] This sacrifice is indeed called *pratiṣṭhā*; when they sacrifice with this sacrifice, everything becomes firmly established (*pratiṣṭhita*).
Now, therefore, regarding the expiations: if a horse should mount a mare, one should subsequently offer a milk-oblation to Vāyu.
Vāyu is indeed the transformer of seed; Vāyu is breath, for breath is the transformer of seed. By means of seed, he thus places seed in him. 13.3.8 [2]
Now, if he should become ill, he should subsequently offer a pap to Pūṣan. Pūṣan indeed rules over cattle;

thus he pleases him who owns cattle and who rules over cattle, and he becomes free from disease. (13.3.8) Now, if he should suffer from a wasting disease, he should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara, using the earth itself as a potsherd.
He should subsequently offer a cake on eight potsherds to Vaiśvānara. This earth, indeed, is Vaiśvānara; it is this very one he thus gratifies, and he becomes free from disease.

Now, if he should suffer from an eye disease, he should subsequently offer a pap to Sūrya. The sun, indeed, is the eye of creatures; for when he rises, then all this world moves. By means of the eye [of the sun], he thus bestows the eye upon him.
That which is the sacrificial pap (caru) is for the sake of the eye, for by means of the eye this self moves.

Now, if he should die in water, he should subsequently offer a barley pap to Varuṇa; for Varuṇa seizes him who dies in water. Whatever deity seizes him, it is that very deity whom he thus gratifies; she [then] bestows [favor] upon him.

He consents to the slaughter for the sake of one who is pleased; he slaughters with her consent. If it should be made of barley, [it is so] because barley belongs to Varuṇa. Now, if it should be lost, he should subsequently perform an offering of three oblations, including a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth.

There is a cake for Vāyu, milk, and a pap for Sūrya. Whatever indeed is lost, it is lost between heaven and earth; the wind blows over it and the sun shines upon it. Nothing whatsoever is lost apart from these deities. This [offering] is specifically the means for finding what is lost. If anything else of his should be lost, he should use this very same [offering].

One should sacrifice; indeed, he thereby finds him. Now, if enemies should find the horse, or if it should die, or if it should perish in water—one should bring another and sprinkle it; that is the expiation in that case.
Prajāpati desired: "May I obtain all desires; may I attain all forms of prosperity. He...

He saw this Aśvamedha, a sacrificial rite lasting three nights; he took it and sacrificed with it. Having sacrificed with it, he obtained all desires and attained all forms of prosperity. Indeed, whoever performs the Aśvamedha obtains all desires and attains all forms of prosperity. 13.4.1 [2]
Regarding this they say: "In which season should one begin? Some say, "One should begin in summer;

for summer is the season of the Kṣatriya, and the Aśvamedha is indeed a Kṣatriya's sacrifice. However, one should rather begin in spring; for spring is the season of the Brāhmaṇa, and whoever sacrifices does so as a Brāhmaṇa.

One sacrifices as if having become a Brāhmaṇī; therefore, one should begin it in the spring alone. Now, six or seven days before that full moon of Phālguna, the officiating priests assemble—the Adhvaryu, the Hotṛ, the Brahman, and the Udgātṛ—and the other priests follow them.
From them, the Adhvaryu prepares the Brahman’s rice-mess for four to eat; its Brāhmaṇa explanation has been stated.

There are four bowls, four handfuls, and four fistfuls—twelvefold in total. Twelve months are a year; the year is everything, and the Aśvamedha is everything. This is for the attainment of everything, for the securing of everything. 13.4.1 [6]
These four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) consume it; their *brāhmaṇa* has been stated. He gives them four thousand [cows];
for a thousand is everything, and the Aśvamedha is everything—for the attainment of everything, for the securing of everything.
And there are four golden *śatamāna* weights of gold; regarding that, it has indeed been stated. 13.4.1. [7]
Then, as the Adhvaryu fastens the gold ornament upon him, he causes him to recite: "Thou art brilliance, pure, immortal.

For gold is indeed brilliance, purity, and immortality; verily, he bestows brilliance, purity, and immortality upon him. [He says: "Protector of life, protect my life! Verily, he bestows life upon him. Then he says to him: "Restrain thy speech. For the sacrifice is speech.
For the very commencement of the sacrifice:

four wives are prepared—the chief queen (*mahiṣī*), the favorite (*vāvātā*), the discarded one (*parivṛktā*), and the daughter-in-law of the *pālāgala*—all wearing gold neck-ornaments (*niṣkin*) and adorned, for the sake of the completeness of the pair. Together with them, he enters the fire-hall by the eastern door.

Through the door, the sacrificer [enters] with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and the wives [enter] behind him. (13.4.1) When the evening oblation has been offered, he lies down to the west of the *gārhapatya* fire, facing north, together with his wife; the others lie down as well. He lies between her thighs without turning over, [thinking]: "By this austerity, may I attain well-being."
"May I attain the conclusion of the year," [he thinks].

(13.4.1) When the morning oblation has been offered, the Adhvaryu offers the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). For the full is indeed everything, and the Aśvamedha is everything; it is for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything. At that [oblation], he releases his speech by means of a choice.

"I grant a boon to Brahmā"—for the boon is indeed everything, and the Aśvamedha is everything; it is for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything. 13.4.1. [11] Now, the gold necklace that is fastened upon him, he gives that to the Adhvaryu; [he gives it] to the Adhvaryu.

"Give, give! He bestows upon himself immortal life; for gold is indeed immortality and life. (13.4.1) Then he performs an offering to Agni for the sake of the paths and so that the opening of the sacrifice may not be spoiled.
Moreover, all the deities have Agni as their mouth, and all desires are centered on the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*); having thus gratified all the gods at the outset, [he proceeds].
"May I obtain all desires.
For this [offering], there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses. The thunderbolt (*vajra*) is indeed fifteenfold; the thunderbolt is vigor.
By means of that very thunderbolt, by means of that vigor, the sacrificer repels evil from the front. The two *ājyabhāga* portions are [verses] slaying Vṛtra.

Vṛtra is indeed evil; for the removal of evil, the invitatory and offering verses for the oblation are recited in a whisper: "Agni is the head of heaven, the summit of the earth, the leader of the sacrifice and of the mid-world. One verse contains the word *mūrdhan* (head), and the other contains the word *sat* (being).
That which shines yonder is indeed the head; [the verse with *mūrdhan*] is for the attainment of that very [head]. And as for the one containing *sat*:
He wins the gods together. The two *saṃyājyā* verses are *virāj*s; for the *virāj* is a metre belonging to all the deities.

"Having gratified all the gods in the Aśvamedha, may I obtain all my desires"—thus [he thinks]. Gold is the sacrificial fee, a hundred-measure piece of gold; its *brāhmaṇa* has been explained. 13.4.1. [14]

Then he offers the oblation to Pūṣan. Pūṣan is indeed the lord of paths; thus he provides this means of well-being for the horse. Moreover, Pūṣan is this earth; he thus makes this earth his protector. For there is neither affliction nor stumbling for one whom she protects on the way; he thus makes this earth his protector. 13.4.1 [15]

For this [sacrifice], there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; Prajāpati is indeed seventeenfold, and the Aśvamedha is Prajāpati—for the attainment of the Aśvamedha itself. The two *ājyabhāga* offerings contain the word "vṛdh" (to increase), for the very increase of the sacrificer. With the verses, "O Pūṣan, in thy service we... and "The path-finding lord of every path, with eloquence...", he offers the oblation in a whisper (*upāṃśu*).

The *yājyā* and *anuṣākya* verses are such that one contains the word "vow" (*vrata*) and the other contains the word "path" (*pathin*). The vow is indeed vigor; it is for the attainment of vigor and for the acquisition of vigor.
Now, as for the verse containing the word "path," he thereby provides a safe journey for the horse. The two *saṃyājyā* verses are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter.
The *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and Prajāpati is speech; the Aśvamedha is Prajāpati. It is for the attainment of the Aśvamedha itself.
A hundred garments is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). A garment is indeed the form of man;

therefore, when they speak of anyone who is well-dressed, they say, "Who is this? for he is perfected by form. Verily, he endows him with form itself. It is a hundred [garments]; man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred powers; verily, he bestows life-span, power, and vigor upon himself. 13.4.2. [1]

While this [sacrificial cow] is being milked, they bring forward a horse—one in which all forms are present, or one that is preeminent in speed, worthy of a thousand, ancient, and such that there is no other yoke-mate for its yoke in the sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā).
As to why it possesses all forms: form is indeed everything, and the Aśvamedha is everything; it is for the attainment of everything.

Now, as for its being "possessing speed" (*javasamṛddha*): speed is indeed vigor; it is for the attainment of vigor, for the acquisition of vigor. Now, as for its being "worth a thousand" (*sahasrārha*): a thousand is indeed everything, and the Aśvamedha is everything;
it is for the attainment of everything, for the acquisition of everything. Now, as for its being "ancient" (*pūrvya*): this [horse] is indeed the unlimited.

Vigor increases so that he may attain the ancient, immeasurable vigor itself. Now, as for the fact that there is no counter-yoke to the southern yoke-pole: this one who shines yonder is indeed that [sun]; it is for the attainment of him that no one at all can be a counter-yoke to him. 13.4.2. [3]
Regarding this, Bhāllabeya said: "This horse should indeed be of two forms, a black-spotted antelope; for it arose from the eye of Prajāpati.
This eye, moreover, is of two forms—both white and black—and thus he endows it with its own proper form. 13.4.2 [4]

Then Sātyayajñi said: "This horse should indeed have three forms: its forepart black, its hindpart white, and it should have a mark like a kṛttikā on its forehead. In that its forepart is black, that is the black part of its eye; and in that its hindpart is white, that is the white part of its eye."
Now, that which has the *kṛttikās* as its mark on the front is the pupil; it is indeed rich in form.

Therefore, whichever one of his [the sacrificer’s] animals may be available—whether it be many-formed, two-formed, or three-formed, provided it has the *kṛttikās* as its mark—that he should sacrifice. However, it should be perfect in speed. 13.4.2 [5]
For him, these guardians are prepared in front: a hundred princes wearing armor; a hundred *rājanya*s carrying quivers;

a hundred sons of charioteers and village headmen (*grāmaṇī*) carrying arrows and shafts; a hundred sons of *kṣatra*-guards and collectors carrying staves; and a hundred horses, worn out and exhausted, upon which they release him and keep watch. 13.4.2. [6]
Then he offers the Sāvitrī sacrifice: a cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ Prasavitṛ. Savitṛ is indeed the impeller;
[he thinks,] "May Savitṛ impel this sacrifice of mine.
For this [sacrifice], there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, and the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are the *vārtraghna* hymns beginning with "He who [governs] all these created beings."

"May the god Savitṛ, possessor of fine jewels, come," is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the oblation, recited in a low voice (*upāṃśu*); the two *virāj* verses are the offering verses (*saṃyājye*).
Gold is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), specifically a hundred-measure (*śatamāna*) piece of gold; its *brāhmaṇa* explanation has already been stated.
While the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*s) are being performed for this [offering], a Brāhmaṇa lute-player (*vīṇāgāthī*) stands to the south.
Striking the *uttara-mandrā* [note], he sings three self-prepared verses: "He sacrificed," "He gave.
The Brāhmaṇa for this has been explained. 13.4.2. Then he offers the second oblation: a cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ Āsavitṛ; for Savitṛ is indeed Āsavitṛ.
"May Savitṛ impel this sacrifice for me," [he says].

For this [offering], there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; the two *ājyabhāga* portions contain the word "seat" (*sad*), whereby he wins the seat. "O God Savitṛ, all things... and "That very God Savitṛ with power..."—these are the invitatory and offering formulas for the oblation, recited in a whisper.

The two *saṃyājyā* verses are in the *anuṣṭubh* metre; the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is silver and gold, for the sake of variety of form, as well as for ascending and not descending. It is a *śatamāna* [weight]; for man has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundred powers (*indriya*).
Thus, he bestows upon himself life, power, and vigor. 13.4.2. [11]

While the *prayāja* offerings for her are being performed, a Brāhmaṇa [plays] the lute. Then he offers the third oblation: a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ of true impulsion (*satyaprasava*). For this indeed is the true impulsion which belongs to Savitṛ; [he offers it thinking: "May he impel this sacrifice for me by means of his true impulsion."

For this [offering], there are exactly seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; the two *ājyabhāga* offerings contain the word "wealth" (*rayi*), for wealth is indeed vigor, [used] for the attainment of vigor and for the securing of vigor. The invitatory and offering verses for the oblation are, in a whisper: "To Viśvadeva, the lord of beings, who is not to be surpassed," and "That of the divine Savitṛ. The two *saṃyājyā* verses are the regular ones.
Thinking, "Let me not depart from the path of the sacrifice," he finally finds firm support in the sacrifice that has been prepared. There are two *triṣṭubh* verses;

for the *triṣṭubh* is indeed power (*vīrya*) in Indra. It is for the attainment of power and vigor. The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is gold, a hundred-measure weight (*śatamāna*) of fine gold; the Brāhmaṇa explanation for this has already been stated. 13.4.2 [14]
While the *prayāja* offerings for her are being performed, a Brahmin [plays] the lute.
When this [offering] has been completed, the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer, having risen, whisper into the right ear of the horse:
"Vibhū by mother, Prabhū by father. The Brāhmaṇa regarding this has already been stated. Then they lead it northward and eastward.

He releases it; for this northern-eastern direction belongs to both gods and men. Thus they place it in its own quarter. Indeed, one who is established in his own abode does not come to harm; [this is] for safety. He says: "O gods, guardians of the quarters, protect this horse consecrated for the sacrifice for the gods. Having been thus addressed—
The human guardians of the quarters are these; then there are the divine Āpyas, Sādhyas, Anvādhyas, and Maruts.
Both these gods and humans, being in agreement and not turning him back, protect him for a year.
As for him whom they do not turn back—he is indeed this one who shines yonder; for who indeed is worthy of turning him back?
If they were to turn him back while he was departing, all this would surely go away; therefore, they guard him without turning him back. He said:
"O guardians of the quarters, those who shall reach the conclusion of this [sacrifice] will become the kingdom, they will be kings."

Those who do not reach the conclusion of this [rite] shall become non-sovereigns; they shall be without a kingdom, and though they be of royal lineage (*rājanya*), the common people (*viś*) shall not consecrate them. Therefore, do not neglect him;
having bathed, you must keep him away from water and from mares.
