Whatever group of Brahmins he may encounter, he should ask them: "O Brahmins, how much do you know of the Aśvamedha? Those who do not know it, he should defeat; for the Aśvamedha is everything. He who, being a Brahmin, does not know the Aśvamedha, does not know this All.
He is no Brahmin; he is indeed to be defeated. "Let us drink [the wine]! they said.
"Then you shall offer food; whatever prepared food there is in the countryside, all that shall be yours.

Your dwelling shall be in the family of the chariot-maker, for that is the abode of the horse. Having released the horse, he spreads a golden cushion to the south of the altar, and upon it the Hotṛ sits down.

To the south of the Hotṛ, on a golden cushion, sits the Sacrificer; to the south [of him], the Brahman and the Udgātṛ on two golden cushions; and in front, facing west, the Adhvaryu on a golden cushion or on a golden plank. 13.4.3. [2]
When they have all sat down, the Adhvaryu gives the direction: "O Hotṛ, recount the beings; seat this sacrificer among the beings.
Thus directed, the Hotṛ addresses the Adhvaryu, intending to recite the Pāriplava narrative: "O Adhvaryu!"—"Havai Hotar! replies the Adhvaryu. 13.4.3. [3]

"Manu Vaivasvata is the king," he says; "his subjects, the humans, are seated here"—thus the householders who are not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*) assemble. He instructs them: "The Ṛgveda is this;
'This is it'—thus he should recite as if explaining a hymn of the Ṛks. Lute-players (*vīṇāgaṇagin*) assemble; the Adhvaryu gives the command to them.

"O you who possess the lute-strings," he says; "sing together with this sacrificer, with the ancient kings who performed good deeds. They sing together with him accordingly. In that they sing together with him thus, they make him share the same world as those ancient kings who performed good deeds. 13.4.3 [4]

Having given the command, the Adhvaryu offers the *prakrama* oblations; or, having traced around the footprint of a horse on the *Anvāhāryapacana* fire, he offers them according to whichever procedure applies there. However, the former is indeed the established rule. Having recited [the formulas] prior to the Sāvitrī sacrifice itself, he offers the *rūpa* oblations once in the Āhavanīya fire, and then in the evening.

While the *dhṛti* oblations are being offered, a kṣatriya who is a lute-player, standing to the south, singing the *uttaramandrā* chant, sings three self-composed verses: "Thus he fought," and "He won that battle.
The Brāhmaṇa explanation for this has been stated. 13.4.3 [6]

Then, on the following day, the second day, when these very Sāvitra offerings have been completed in the same manner, the procedure is as follows: "Adhvaryu! says the Hotṛ; "Havai Hotar! replies the Adhvaryu. [The Hotṛ] says, "King Yama Vaivasvata;
his subjects are the Pitṛs; they are seated here. The elders who have gathered there he instructs in the sacrificial formulas (yajūṃṣi).

He should recite the section of the *Yajus* formulas beginning with "This is that Veda," as if explaining it, and the Adhvaryu should likewise give the summons; he does not, however, offer the *prakrama* oblations.
Then, on the third day, when these same offerings have been completed, this same procedure applies, [beginning with the call]: "O Adhvaryu! indeed.
"Hotṛ!"—thus says the Adhvaryu; "Varuṇa Āditya the King! he says; "The Gandharvas are his subjects; they sit here.

Young and handsome men are gathered there; he points them out [to the Hotṛ], saying, "The Atharvans are the Veda; this is it. He should run along as if explaining a single section of the Atharvans; even so does the Adhvaryu.
He gives the command, but he does not step forward to offer the oblations.

13.4.3.[8] Then, on the fourth day, when these same offerings have been completed, this is the procedure: "O Adhvaryu! says the Hotṛ; "Havai Hotar! replies the Adhvaryu. "King Soma Vaiṣṇava," he says, "his subjects are the Apsarases; they are sitting here."

Beautiful young women assemble; he instructs them: "This is the Veda of the Aṅgirases. He recites one section of the Aṅgirases as if explaining it. 13.4.3 [9] Then, on the fifth day, when these same offerings have been completed, this is the procedure: "O Adhvaryu!"—thus he calls out.
"Hotar!"—thus the Adhvaryu says, "Arbuda, son of Kadrū, the king; his subjects are the serpents, and they sit here.

The serpents and those who know all things have assembled there; he instructs them, saying, "This is the Veda of Serpent-knowledge (Sarpavidyā)," and he recites as if explaining a single section of the Sarpavidyā.

Then, on the sixth day, when these same offerings have been completed, the procedure is exactly as follows: "Adhvaryu! says the Hotṛ; "Havai Hotar! replies the Adhvaryu. "Kubera Vaiśravaṇa is the king," he says, "and the Rākṣasas are his subjects; they are staying here. Then the *selagas* and *pādakṛts* assemble, and he instructs them: "This is the Veda, the knowledge of the divine folk (*devajana-vidyā*)."
He should recite the first section of the *Devajanavidyā* as if explaining it.

13.4.3.[11] Then, on the seventh day, when these offerings have been completed in this same manner, the procedure is as follows: "Adhvaryu! says the Hotṛ; "Havai Hotar! replies the Adhvaryu. "The Asita Dhānvas are the people (*viś*)," he says; "the Asuras are their people," [he says]; "these Kusīdins sit here."

When they have become calm, he instructs them: "This Veda is an illusion (*māyā*"; he may perform some kind of illusion, and in this very manner the Adhvaryu gives the summons; he does not offer the *prakrama* oblations). 13.4.3.
[12] Now, on the eighth day, when these same offerings have been completed, this is the procedure: "O Adhvaryu!"—thus indeed [he says].

"Hotṛ! says the Adhvaryu; "Matsya Sāmmada, the king," he says; "his subjects are the water-dwellers; they sit here. Fish and fishermen have gathered there, and he points them out, saying, "The Itihāsa is the Veda; this is it. He should recount some such Itihāsa; in this very manner the Adhvaryu gives the command, but he does not perform the *prakrama* oblations. 13.4.3. [13]

Then, on the ninth day, when these very sacrifices have been completed in this same manner, the procedure is as follows: "O Adhvaryu! says the Hotṛ; "O Hotṛ! replies the Adhvaryu. [The Hotṛ] says, "Tārkṣya Vaipaśyata is the king; his subjects are the birds, and they are seated here. Now, both birds and those skilled in the science of birds (vāyovidyika) have assembled there, and he instructs them: "This is that ancient Veda."
He should recite some portion of the *Purāṇa*; in this very manner the Adhvaryu gives the summons, but he does not offer the *prakrama* oblations. 13.4.3.

[14] Then, on the tenth day, when these same sacrifices have been completed, this is the procedure: "O Adhvaryu! says the Hotṛ; "O Hotṛ! replies the Adhvaryu. "Dharma is King Indra," he says; "the gods are his subjects; they sit here"—referring to the learned *śrotriyas*.
Those who are without a teacher become tranquil; he instructs them with the Sāmans, saying, "This is the Veda, this is that.
He should recite a decade of Sāmans; in this very manner the Adhvaryu gives the command, for he does not offer the *prakrama* oblations.
This is the *pāriplava*: it recounts all kingdoms, all subjects, all Vedas, all gods, and all [beings].
He indeed attains union with and residence in the same world as all these beings;

he attains sovereignty and lordship over all the people; he acquires all the Vedas; having gratified all the gods, he finally finds firm support in all beings—this is for him whose Hotṛ-priest recites this Pāriplava narrative.

This very same narrative, being known thus, revolves repeatedly throughout the year; because it revolves again and again, it is called the *pāriplava*. He recites thirty-six ten-day periods (*daśāha*);
the *bṛhatī* consists of thirty-six syllables, and cattle belong to the *bṛhatī*; verily, by means of the *bṛhatī*, he wins cattle for him. 13.4.4. [1]

When the year has elapsed, having performed the consecration (*dīkṣā*) and offered the animal sacrifice to Prajāpati, the *iṣṭi* sacrifices are concluded; some say that one should perform them in the fires of the domestic priest (*purohita*). But how could one who is consecrated perform [ordinary] sacrifices? There are twelve days of consecration, twelve days of *upasad*, and three days of *sutyā*; thus it amounts to the *triṇava* (twenty-seven). The *triṇava* is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*); the horse is the nobility (*kṣatra*), and the Rājanya is the nobility.
The kṣatra is indeed secured by the thunderbolt; thus, by means of the thunderbolt itself, he secures the kṣatra.
(13.4.4) When the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering has been completed and speech has been released in the evening, the lute-players assemble.
The adhvaryu gives them the direction, saying, "O lute-players, sing together with the gods for this sacrificer. Him—
They chant together in this manner.
Day after day, when speech has been released, at the conclusion of the Agniṣomīya offerings and once the Vasatīvarī waters have been carried around, they chant together with him.
By chanting together with the gods, they thus make him share the same world as the gods.

In the same manner, when the *sutyā* days have been completed day after day by Prajāpati, and when the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice has finally concluded with the *vasatīvarī* waters, they sing together with him using Prajāpati; thus, by means of Prajāpati itself, they finally make him share the same world. 13.4.4 [5]

There are twenty-one sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), all of them twenty-one *aratni* in height. The central post, standing near the fire, is made of *rājjudāla* wood; on both sides of it are two made of *pitu-dāru* wood. There are six made of *bilva* wood—three on this side and three on that side; six made of *khadira* wood—three on this side and three on that side; and six made of *pālāśa* wood—three on this side and three on that side. 13.4.4. [6]

Now, as for why these sacrificial posts are thus: when the vital breaths had departed from Prajāpati, his body began to swell. The phlegm that was in it flowed out together and burst forth from the middle of the nose; that became this tree, the *rajjudāla*. Therefore, it is called *śleṣmaṇa*, for it is indeed from phlegm.

He became equal [to them]; with that very form he thus causes him to prosper. In that the one standing nearest the fire (agniṣṭha) exists—since the one nearest the fire is the middle among the sacrificial posts, and the nose is the middle among the vital breaths—he thereby places him in his own proper abode.
Now, when that brilliance consisting of water existed, that which was its fragrance flowed together with it and burst forth from the eye;

that became this tree, the *pītu* wood. Therefore, it is fragrant, for it originated from fragrance; and therefore it is glowing, for it originated from brilliance. By means of that very form, he thus causes him to prosper.
In that those two [cups] are on both sides of the one belonging to Agni, therefore these two eyes are on both sides of the nose; he thus places them in their own proper abode.
Then, as for what was the *kuntāpa*—that which was the marrow, having flowed together with it, burst forth from the ear; that is this [cup].
The Bilva became the Vanaspati; therefore, within its fruit, everything is edible.

For that reason, it is yellowish, for its marrow is yellowish; he thus endows it with that very form. The two [pillars] made of Pītudāru wood are on the inside, and those made of Bilva wood are on the outside; for the eyes are on the inside, and the outer parts are on the outside.
He thus places them in their own abode, the ear itself.

From his bones the *khadira* tree came into being; therefore it is hard and full of pith, for bone is, as it were, hard. He thus endows it with that very form. Those made of *bilva* wood are on the inside, and those of *khadira* on the outside, for [the marrow] is inside.
The marrow is the outermost bones; he thus places them each in its own proper abode.
From his flesh the *palāśa* tree arose; therefore it is full of juice and has red juice, for flesh is like blood.
By means of that very form, he thus makes him complete. The *khadira* wood is used within, while the *palāśa* is on the outside.

For the bones are internal and the flesh is external; he thus places them each in their own proper location. Now, as to why there are twenty-one [posts]: they are twenty-one cubits long, for this one who shines (the sun) is the twenty-first—twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first; he is the Aśvamedha. This is it.

Having thus prepared this Prajāpati, the sacrifice, in its entirety, Prajāpati offers twenty-one animals dedicated to Agni and Soma; their ritual procedure is the same—this is the ritual of the preceding day. 13.5.1 [1]

Now, in the morning, there is for Gotama the four-plus chant (caturuttara-stoma). Its *bahiṣpavamāna* is on four verses; the *ājya* chants are on eight verses each; the midday *pavamāna* is on twelve verses; the *pṛṣṭha* chants are on sixteen verses; the *ārbhava-pavamāna* is on twenty verses; and the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* is on twenty-four verses. 13.5.1. [2]
Regarding this, some perform a four-fold *sāman* for the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*, asserting that it is neither an *agniṣṭoma* nor an *ukthya*.

If they should do so, having recited the *stotriya* together with its *anurūpa*, he should recite the *rathantara* as the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* and the *rāthantara-śastra*; thus it becomes an *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice, and by means of it, him—
"He prospers in the world.

(13.5.1.3) "There are twenty-one *savanīya* animals, all dedicated to Agni; their ritual procedure is the same," so say some. However, one should indeed offer two sets of eleven [animals], for the attainment of whatever desire there may be regarding the sets of eleven. (13.5.1.4)
When the Agniṣṭoma has been completed and the Vasatīvarī waters have been carried around, the Adhvaryu offers the food-oblations.

The Brāhmaṇa for these has been stated: "To Prāṇa, svāhā! To Apāna, svāhā! with twelve Anuvākas. There are twelve months in a year; the year is everything, and the Aśvamedha is everything—for the attainment of everything.
For the attainment of everything.
The middle day is the twenty-one-fold; yonder sun is indeed the twenty-one-fold, and he is the Aśvamedha.
By means of its own Stoma, it establishes it in its own deity; therefore, it is the twenty-one-fold.

Moreover, as to why it is the twenty-first: man indeed consists of twenty-one parts—ten fingers of the hands, ten toes of the feet, and the self is the twenty-first. Thus, by means of this twenty-first self, he becomes established in that twenty-first foundation;
therefore, it is the twenty-first. 13.5.1 [7]

Or rather, as to why it is the twenty-onefold [stoma]: the twenty-onefold is indeed the foundation of the *stomas*. On this day, many various kinds of ritual acts are performed; thus, when many various acts are performed on this day, he should perform them so that they are established upon this twenty-onefold foundation.

Therefore, this very twenty-first day [is so called]. 13.5.1. [8] Its morning pressing: the Hotṛ, having recited the fivefold *ājya* hymn beginning with "I think of that Agni who is the Vasu," recites the one-day (*ekāhika*) [laud] as a supplement, as well as both the *bārhata* and the *mādhucandasa* *prauga* lauds, in triplets.

Whatever desire is expressed in the *bārhata* *prauga* and whatever desire is expressed in the *mādhucandasa*, for the attainment of both those desires, the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) is prepared.
Now, therefore, follows the midday pressing (*mādhyandinaṃ savanam*): the *aticandāḥ* verse is the opening hymn of the *marutvatīya* litany, [beginning with] "In the *trikadruka* cups... (RV 8.2.41).
The *mahiṣa* [verse] is "yavāśiram"; this *atichandas* is indeed the pre-eminent among meters, and the *aśvamedha* is the pre-eminent among sacrifices;

thus it is for the attainment of the *aśvamedha*. This very [verse], when recited three times, becomes a *tricha*; thereby he obtains that desire which is [fulfilled by] a *tricha*. "This pressed juice, O Vasu..."—this is the permanent *anucara*, the extension of the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*). Thus.

"For you, O Soma, in the exhilaration, are the protector of the one who presses [the juice] and has spread the sacrificial grass"—having recited these *pañkti* verses and those consisting of six feet, he places the *nivid* in the *aikāhika* [chant]; such is the *marutvatīya*.
Now, therefore, regarding the *niṣkevalya*: the *mahānāmnī* verses constitute the *pṛṣṭha*; he recites them along with their *anurūpa* and *pragātha*.

"All desires indeed are in the Mahānāmnī verses; all desires are in the Aśvamedha. For the attainment of all desires, [the priest] recites "Indra has grown for exhilaration" and "This prayer has helped you in the battles against Vṛtra," and having recited both the *paṅkti* and the six-footed verses, he places the *nivid* in the one-day rite (*aikāhika*). Thus, the midday pressing is prepared. 13.5.1. [11]

Now, therefore, follows the third pressing. The *aticandās* verse, "To the god Savitṛ, the impeller, with songs... (*abhi tvā deva savitāram oṇyoḥ*), is the opening hymn (*pratipad*) for the Vaiśvadeva laud; its explanatory passage (*brāhmaṇa*) is the same as that of the preceding one. The following verse, "Thee, O god Savitṛ... (*abhi tvā deva savitar*), is the *anucara*; it contains the word "over" (*abhi*) and is thus a form of overcoming. Then comes the Sāvitra verse: "Up has risen this god Savitṛ, the friend of the house... (*ud u ṣya devaḥ savitā damūnāḥ*).

Having recited the *śastra* for the one-day rite (*aikāhika*), he places the *nivid*; having recited the four-verse hymn addressed to Heaven and Earth beginning with "The great Heaven and Earth, the eldest here," he places the *nivid* for the one-day rite;
having recited the *śastra* addressed to the Ṛbhus beginning with "Ṛbhu, Vibhvan, Vāja, and Indra have perceived us," he places the *nivid* for the one-day rite;
[and] with the verse beginning "Who now, O Mitra and Varuṇa, seeking the Law... he places the *nivid*.
Having recited the Vaiśvadeva [śastra], one places the *nivid* for the one-day rite (*aikāhika*); thus it is called the Vaiśvadeva. 13.5.1.
[12] Now, therefore, regarding the Āgnimāruta: having recited the Vaiśvānara [verse], "The head of heaven, the messenger of earth," one places the *nivid* for the one-day rite;
and having recited the Māruta [verse], "O Rudras, accompanied by Indra, being of one accord," one places the *nivid* for the one-day rite.
Having recited the nine-verse hymn addressed to Jātavedas beginning with "He places this guest among you, awakening at dawn," he inserts the *nivid* according to the one-day (*aikāhika*) ritual.
Now, as to why the *nivid*-insertions belong to the one-day rites: the Jyotiṣṭoma is indeed a firm foundation; it is for the sake of not falling away from that foundation. 13.5.1. [13]
These are his sacrificial animals: a horse, a hornless goat, and a gayal—these fifteen are the animals bound to the limbs; their Brāhmaṇa has been explained.
Now these are the wild ones: for the spring he immolates francolins, for the summer sparrows, and for the rains partridges; their Brāhmaṇa has likewise been explained. 13.5.1. [14]
Then he slaughters twenty-one animals for each of the deities of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, making twenty-one for each.

[The opponent argues: "All the gods are as numerous as the deities of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; since all desires are contained within the Aśvamedha, one should satisfy all the gods so that one may obtain all desires. One should not do so. 13.5.1. [15]

One should immolate exactly seventeen animals at the central sacrificial post; Prajāpati is seventeenfold, the All is seventeenfold, and the Aśvamedha is the All—for the attainment of the All, for the securing of the All. On the other posts, sixteen each;
for this All consists of sixteen parts, and the Aśvamedha is the All—for the attainment of the All, for the securing of the All.

Thirteen by thirteen he offers in the forest-enclosures and in the spaces; thirteen months are a year; the year is everything; the Aśvamedha is everything—for the attainment of everything, for the securing of everything. 13.5.1.
[16] Now, before the Bahiṣpavamāna chant, they lead up the horse after washing it; with that [horse] they proceed to the Pavamāna chant.

Regarding this, the Brāhmaṇa has been stated: when the Bahiṣpavamāna has been chanted, they lead the horse to the Āstāva. If it should either smell the barley or turn about, he should know, "My sacrifice is successful. Having brought it near, the Adhvaryu says, "O Hotṛ, chant the hymn! The Hotṛ chants the hymn for it with eleven verses. 13.5.1. [17]
With the verse, "When you first cried out at birth," he recites the first verse thrice and the last verse thrice; these amount to fifteen.

The thunderbolt (*vajra*) is indeed fifteenfold and is vigor; by means of this thunderbolt, this vigor, the sacrificer repels evil from the front. By means of this thunderbolt, this vigor, the sacrificer repels evil from the front.
Verily, that thunderbolt is bestowed upon the sacrificer himself against whom he intends to strike; [he recites]:
"The swift steed has gone forward to the place of slaughter; the racer has gone forward to the highest station.
Having lifted these [verses], he inserts this hymn, "May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, and the others not [abandon us]," for one who is not yet fit for the sacrifice.
"Thirty-four are the steeds of the friend of the gods"—thus some place this verse before the *vaṅkris*.
They do so thinking, "Lest we place the *praṇava* in a place that is not its proper abode," and also, "Lest we separate the singular number from the plural.
One should not do so; rather, one should insert this hymn together [with the others]: "The swift steed has come near to the seat... and "O steed... and so forth.
"Go forth to that which is the supreme dwelling-place"—having said this, he recites whatever remains of the *adhrigu* formula.
They spread out for the horse a garment, an undergarment, and gold; upon that they immolate it. When the animals have been immolated...
The wives rise up with the water for washing the feet— four wives, a maiden as the fifth, and four hundred female attendants.
When the washing of the feet is completed, they cause the chief queen to lie down beside the horse, and then they clothe them both with the upper garment.
“They completely cover [it] in the heavenly world; may you two cover [it],” he says—for that where they quiet the victim is indeed the heavenly world.

He draws out the horse’s penis and places it in the lap of the chief queen, saying, “May the vigorous stallion, the depositor of seed, deposit seed,” for the sake of the completeness of the pair. 13.5.2. [3]

While the two of them are lying there, the sacrificer addresses the horse with the words, "O you with broad thighs, cover your anus! No one at all addresses him in return, lest there be someone who acts as a rival to the sacrificer. Then the Adhvaryu addresses a young girl with the words, "O girl, hey! Hey! O girl, who is that little bird?"* 13.5.2 [4] *The commentary notes that this is said because the horse is considered a male bird (*śakunti*). The *yakāsakau* refers to the two testicles. The absence of a response from anyone else is a ritual requirement to maintain the sacrificer's exclusive status. The maiden retorts to him: "O Adhvaryu! Hey, hey, Adhvaryu! Who is that little bird over there? (13.5.2). Then the Brahman addresses the Mahiṣī: "O Mahiṣī! Hey, hey, Mahiṣī! Both your mother and your father climb to the top of the tree. For her, there are a hundred princesses as attendants; they [address] the Brahman.

They mock him, saying, "O Brahmin! Hāya! Hāya! O Brahmin! Your mother and your father are playing at the top of the tree! (13.5.2[6]) Then the Udgātṛ mocks the favorite wife, saying, "O favorite! Hāya! Hāya! O favorite! Make her rise up!"

A hundred Rajanya women are her attendants; they mock the Udgātṛ, saying: "O Udgātṛ, ho! Ho! O Udgātṛ, lift up this man with the highest praise! (13.5.2). Then the Hotṛ mocks the Parivṛktā, saying: "O Parivṛktā, ho! Ho! O Parivṛktā, as for this woman who breaks through the narrow pass..."

Thus, for her, there are a hundred daughters of charioteers and village headmen as attendants; they mock the Hotṛ, saying: "O Hotṛ, come! O Hotṛ, come! O Hotṛ, when the gods [behold] the one with pendulous testicles!
(13.5.2.8) Then the Kṣattṛ mocks the Pālāgalī, saying: "O Pālāgalī, come! O Pālāgalī, come! When the deer eats the barley..."

"He does not think much of the fat [meat]," she says; for her, there are a hundred daughters of the *kṣatra-saṅgrahītṛ*s as attendants, and they mock the *kṣattṛ*: "O *kṣattṛ*, come, come, O *kṣattṛ*! When the deer eats the barley, he does not think much of the fat. 13.5.2. [9]

These incantations are indeed the attainment of all speech; all desires are contained in the Aśvamedha. Thinking, "May we obtain all desires by means of all speech," they cause the Mahiṣī to rise. Thereupon, they return by the same way they came.
Then the others recite at the end the verse containing the word *surabhi*: "I have performed the praise of Dadhikrāvan. (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 13.5.2.10)
Indeed, the life-sustaining deities depart from those who either speak impurely at the sacrifice or utter speech that is not fit for the sacrifice;

they purify speech itself for the sake of sacrificing to the gods and so that the deities do not depart. As for the omentum of the *gomṛga* and that of the hornless goat (*ajā-tūpara*), they place them upon the horse and bring them forward, saying, "There is no omentum of the horse," but it is not so.
One should perform this in the very presence of the horse; one should take the fat from those [limbs] that are well-known, while the others are [taken] otherwise.
(13.5.2.11) When the omenta have been cooked, having performed the offerings with the *svāhākṛti* formulas, they return westward and engage in the *brahmodya* (theological debate) in the *sadas*.
Having entered by the eastern door, they sit down separately according to their respective hearths (*dhiṣṇya*). (13.5.2.12)
The Hotṛ asks the Adhvaryu: "Who, indeed, wanders alone? He replies to him: "The Sun wanders alone.
(13.5.2.13) Then the Adhvaryu asks the Hotṛ: "What light is equal to the Sun? He replies to him: "The Brahman is the light equal to the Sun. (13.5.2.14)
Then the Brahman asks the Udgātṛ: "I ask you for the sake of knowledge, O friend of the gods. He replies to him: "I am indeed within those three steps.
(13.5.2[15]) Then the Udgātṛ asks the Brahman: "Into how many has the Person entered? He replies to him: "Into five."
"The Puruṣa has entered" (13.5.2.16). When this [verse] has been recited, they rise and, from the *sadas*, proceed eastward toward the sacrificer along the front of the two *havirdhāna* sheds.
Having approached him as he sits in his place, they sit down around him.

13.5.2.[17] The Hotṛ asks the Adhvaryu: "What was the first thought? He replies to him: "The sky was the first thought. 13.5.2.[18] Then the Adhvaryu asks the Hotṛ: "Who is this reddish-brown one? He replies to him: "A goat is this reddish-brown one. 13.5.2.[19]

Then the Brahman asks the Udgātṛ: "How many are its stations? How many are its syllables? He replies to him: "Six are its stations; a hundred are its syllables. (13.5.2) Then the Udgātṛ asks the Brahman: "Who knows the navel of this world? He replies to him:
"I know the navel of this world," [he says].
(13.5.2.21) Then the sacrificer asks the Adhvaryu: "I ask you about the furthest limit of the earth.
He should reply to him: "This altar is the furthest limit of the earth. (13.5.2.22)
The Brahmodya is indeed the attainment of all speech; all desires are contained in the Aśvamedha.
[Thinking], "By means of all speech, may we obtain all desires," (the Adhvaryu acts).
When the Brahmodya has been uttered, the Adhvaryu enters with a golden vessel the Mahiman cup belonging to Prajāpati.
He takes the draught; for this, the *puroruc* is: "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning. Then its *puro'nuvākyā* is:

"Subhūḥ, the self-existent, the first... The *praisha* is: "Let the Hotṛ sacrifice to Prajāpati. The Hotṛ sacrifices with: "O Prajāpati, none other than you [created] these... At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the oblation with: "That greatness of yours which is in the day and in the year..."
"He came into being"—thus he does not perform the *anuvaṣaṭ* call, for he offers it as a complete oblation (*sarvahuta*). Now, therefore, follows the offering of the omenta.
They should proceed separately until the omentum of the Vaiśvadeva; once the omentum of the Vaiśvadeva has been offered, they should offer the others following that.
Thus said Satyakāma Jābāla: "The Viśve are indeed all."
"The gods satisfy them according to their respective deities," [so it is said].
When the offering for Indra and Agni has been made, they should then offer the others after it; thus said Saumapa and Mānutantavya:
"Indra and Agni are indeed all the gods; thus one satisfies them according to their respective deities."

"Once the omentum of the body has been offered, they should offer the other parts following that," so said Śailāli; "for he thus gratifies them according to their respective deities. "Ka is indeed Prajāpati, and all the gods follow after Prajāpati;
therefore, he thus gratifies them according to their respective deities," [so said another]. 13.5.3. [3]

"Having offered to the twenty-one deities of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices and having divided [the oblation] into twenty-one parts, they should proceed," so said Bhāllabeya; "for as many as there are all the gods, so many are the deities of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; thus he gratifies them according to their respective deities. 13.5.3. [4]

"They should proceed separately," said Indrota Śaunaka; "for why should they hasten? In that very way they gratify them according to their respective deities. This was their statement, but the established rule is indeed otherwise. Then Yājñavalkya said: "They should proceed with the offerings to Prajāpati only once."
By means of verses addressed to the gods individually, he thus gratifies them according to their respective deities; he reaches the conclusion of the sacrifice directly and does not stumble.
When the omenta have been offered, the two Adhvaryu priests enter with a silver vessel for the subsequent Mahiman cup dedicated to Prajāpati.
He takes the cup for it with the verse, "He who by his greatness [rules] over all that breathes and blinks. The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* are inverted for the sake of avoiding stale repetition.
This is the same *praiṣa*. When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers with the verse, "That majesty of thine which was produced in the night of the year.
He does not perform the *anuvaṣaṭ* offering; the *brāhmaṇa* regarding this has already been stated. 13.5.3. [7]
They do not cut portions from the other animals with the *tedanī* knife; they cut the portion of the horse from the right side, while they cut the portions of the other animals from the left side.
They cut the portions of the other animals on branches of the *plakṣa* tree, and those of the horse on branches of the *vetasa* reed. 13.5.3 [8]

Regarding this, Sātyayajñi said: "They should do otherwise; they should not depart from the path. However, the established rule is that the sacrifice is an Ukthya; by it, one prospers in the intermediate world (*antarikṣaloka*). The final day is an Atirātra with all the Stomas. Indeed, the Atirātra with all the Stomas is everything, and the Aśvamedha is everything; it is for the attainment of everything.
For the attainment of everything.
Its *bahiṣpavamāna* is the *trivṛt*; the *ājya* stotras are *pañcadaśa*; the midday *pavamāna* is *saptadaśa*; the *pṛṣṭha* stotras are *ekaviṃśa*; and the third [turn] is *triṇava*.
The *pavamāna* chant is the *trayastrimśa*; the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* consists of the *ekaviṃśa* stotras; the *ṣoḍaśin* is the *ekaviṃśa*;

the night-chant is the *pañcadaśa*; the *sandhi* is the *trivṛt*. That which belongs to the second day of the *ṣaḍaha* (six-day rite) with its *pṛṣṭha* chants—that is the *caturtha* (the fourth part);
and the *atirātra* sacrifice. By means of this sacrifice, he prospers in that world. 13.5.3. [10]

"There are twenty-one Savanīya animals, all dedicated to Agni; their ritual procedure is the same," so say some. However, one should indeed immolate these twenty-four bovine animals for twelve deities; twelve months are a year, and the year is everything—the Aśvamedha is everything—for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything. 13.5.4. [1]

By means of this, Hendruta Daivāpa Śaunaka caused Janamejaya Pārikṣita to perform the sacrifice; having sacrificed with it, he cast off all evil-doing and all the murder of a Brahmin. Indeed, whoever performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice casts off all evil-doing and all the murder of a Brahmin. 13.5.4[2]
This has been sung in a verse: "Upon the Āsandīvat [altar], Janamejaya bound for the gods a dappled horse—gold-adorned, eating grain, wearing a green garland.
These same two preceding days and the Jyotis Atirātra constitute the Bhīmasena sacrifice; these same two preceding days...

Gaura performed the Atirātra sacrifice; then Ugrasena performed these same two preceding days [the Agniṣṭoma and Ukthya]. Āyu performed the Atirātra sacrifice; then Śruta-sena performed [these]. These were the descendants of Parikṣit. This has been celebrated in a verse: "The meritorious descendants of Parikṣit, performing the Aśvamedha sacrifices, cast off their evil karma from one end to the other by means of their meritorious deeds. (13.5.4)
These same two preceding days and the *Abhijit* *Atirātra*: with this, Para Āṭṇāra, the Kausalya king, performed the sacrifice.
Regarding this, it has been sung in a *gāthā*: "Para, the son of Aṭṇāra, bound the horse fit for sacrifice;
Hairaṇyanābha, the Kausalya, bestowed the full quarters [of the earth]. 13.5.4. [5]
These same two previous days [and] the Viśvajit Atirātra—by means of this, Purukutsa, the son of Ikṣvāku, performed the sacrifice for Durgaha.
Therefore, this was spoken by the seer: "Our fathers were there; they were the seven seers when [the victim] was bound for Durgaha. (13.5.4)
These same two preceding days [are performed] with the Mahāvrata and Atirātra; with that, Marutta Āvikṣita, the king of the Āyogavas, sacrificed.
Then the Maruts became his waiters, Agni his steward, and the Viśve Devas his courtiers. This has been celebrated in a Gāthā: "The Maruts were the waiters in the house of Marutta."

"Agni is the *kṣattṛ* (steward) for Āvikṣita; the Viśve Devas are the members of the assembly (*sabhāsadaḥ*). Indeed, the Maruts are his servers, Agni is the steward, and the Viśve Devas are the members of the assembly for him who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice.

These same [deities] preside over the two preceding days, and the Aptoryāma Atirātra follows. With this [sacrifice], King Krivya of the Pañcālas performed the sacrifice; the Krivis are [his descendants].

Indeed, they formerly called them the Pañcālas; this has been celebrated in a verse: "The Pāñcāla king, superior to many men, sacrificed a horse fit for the *medha* at Parivakrā, with a sacrificial fee of a hundred thousand.
Then, by the second [verse]: "A thousand, ten thousand, and twenty-five hundred were there from every direction of the Pañcālas."
"The Brahmins who divided [it]," so it is said (13.5.4.9).
The Agniṣṭoma is the Trivṛt; the Ukthya is the Pañcadaśa; the third day is the Saptadaśa with its Ukthas;
the Ṣoḍaśin is the Ekaviṃśa; the night is the Pañcadaśa; the Sandhi is the Trivṛt—this is perfected as the Anuṣṭubh. By means of this, Dhvasan [attained his goal].
The King of the Matsyas performed a sacrifice at Dvaitavana; this is that very lake Dvaitavana about which this verse is sung:
"Fourteen horses, winners in battle, did the King of Dvaitavana bind for Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra; therefore it is called the lake Dvaitavana. (13.5.4)

The Pavamāna stotras are twenty-four-versed, revolving around the nine-versed; the Pavamāna stotras are forty-four-versed, revolving around the twenty-one-versed; the Pavamāna stotras are forty-eight-versed, revolving around the thirty-three-versed.
The Uktha-stotras consist of thirty-two-versed verses, and the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is twenty-one-versed.

The sixteenth [night], the fifteenth night, and the Trivṛt as the junction—this is Viṣṇu’s stride. By means of this very sacrifice, Bharata, the son of Duḥṣanta, performed the rite; having sacrificed with it, he attained this preeminence which belongs to the Bharatas. This has been celebrated in a verse: "Bharata [conquered] seventy-eight..."
"The son of Duṣyanta bound fifty-five horses for Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, along the Yamunā at the Gaṅgā.

[13.5.4.12] "Then, by means of the second [verse], King Sudyumna, having bound one hundred and thirty-three sacrificial horses, stood firm; he surpassed others who were more skilled in magic. [13.5.4.13]
Then, by the third [verse], it is said that the Apsaras Śakuntalā bore Bharata; he, having conquered the entire earth, brought for Indra more than a thousand sacrificial horses.
Then, by the fourth [verse]: "Great indeed is this day of Bharata; neither those before nor those after him have reached heaven like a mortal."
"The five men could not lift him with their two arms.
(13.5.4[15]) Ṛṣabha Yājñatura, the king of the Śviknas, performed a sacrifice with the Ekaviṃśastoma. Regarding this, it is sung in a verse:
"While Yājñatura Ṛṣabha was sacrificing, the people, having obtained wealth at the Aśvamedha, divided it among themselves."

"Regarding the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā): King Śoṇa Sātrāsāha of the Pañcālas performed a sacrifice with the thirty-three-fold hymn-form (trayastriṃśastoma). This has been celebrated in a verse concerning Sātrāsāha: 13.5.4.[16]
"Through the horse-sacrifice performed by the sacrificer, the thirty-three [gods] of Tūrvaśa rise up—six thousand armored warriors," so it is said.

13.5.4.[17] Then, with the second [verse]: "Six times six thousand [warriors], O son of Koka, rise up at your sacrifice—the thirty-three [gods] and six thousand armored warriors," so it is said. 13.5.4.[18]

Then, when King Susrajit Pāñcāla, the son of Sātrāsaha, was performing the sacrifice, Indra rejoiced in the *soma* and the Brahmins were satisfied with wealth. Śatānīka Sātrājita, having seized the horse of the king of Kāśī, performed the Govinata sacrifice. Thus [ends the section]. 13.5.4. [19]
Those who had been excluded from speech and thought, having taken up the Soma-draught, said, "We shall establish the fires.
Its arrangement is as follows: the Pavamāna stotras are twenty-four-fold; the Abhyāvarta is threefold; the Pavamāna stotras are forty-four-fold;
the Ājya stotras are twenty-one-fold; the Uktha stotras are twenty-seven-fold; the Pṛṣṭha stotras are twenty-one-fold; and the [Agniṣṭoma] stotras are thirty-six-fold.

The Pavamāna stotras lead up to the Trayastrimśa; the Ukthas have the Ekavimśa as their Agniṣṭoma-sāman; the Ṣoḍaśin has the Ekavimśa; the night-chants have the Pañcadaśa; and the Sandhi-stotra has the Trivṛt.
Regarding this, it is sung in a Gāthā: "Śatānīka Sātrājita took the sacrificial horse from the Samantās."
"Bharata [performed] the sacrifice of the Kāśīs, as [did] the Satvats"—thus [it is said].

Then, with the second [verse], Śatānīka, having seized Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sacrificial white horse that wandered at will all around, [offered it], saying: "Śatānīka has conquered the ten-month-old horse by means of Govinata. 13.5.4.[22–23]

"Now, on the fourth [day], it was said: 'Today, among the Bharatas, neither those of old nor those of later times have reached heaven as mortals reach it with their two wings—neither the seven nor the nine.
Now, therefore, regarding the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*): [they consist of] that which belongs to the kingdom other than the land and the men, up to the middle.
The eastern quarter belongs to the Brahman from the wealth of the Brahmin; the southern to the Hotṛ; the western to the Brahman;
the northern to the Adhvaryu; and the same [quarters] belong to the Udgātṛ. Thus are the Hotṛkāḥ included.
When the *udayanīyā* offering has been completed, he immolates twenty-one barren cows as the *anūbandhyā*.
[The cakes] belong to Mitra-Varuṇa, to the Viśve Devas, and to Bṛhaspati; this is for the attainment of these deities. Now, as to why those belonging to Bṛhaspati are last:

Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; thus, he finally establishes himself in the Brahman. (13.5.4) Now, as to why there are twenty-one: he who shines yonder is indeed the twenty-first; [there are] twelve months...
The five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun as the twenty-first— this is the perfect correspondence.

When the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice has been completed, they give as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) four wives with a maiden as the fifth, and four hundred female attendants, according to what has been previously agreed upon.

Then, in the following year, he sacrifices with the seasonal animal victims (*ṛtupaśu*): six dedicated to Agni in the spring, six to Indra in the summer, six to Parjanya or the Maruts in the rainy season,
six to Mitra-Varuṇa in the autumn, and six to Indra-Viṣṇu in the winter.
With six [sacrifices] for Indra and Bṛhaspati in the cool season, there are six seasons, which constitute the year; thus he finds firm support in the seasons, in the year itself.

These animals amount to thirty-six; the *bṛhatī* meter consists of thirty-six syllables, and upon the *bṛhatī* the heavenly world is established. Therefore, in the end, by means of the *bṛhatī* meter itself, he finds firm support in the heavenly world. 13.6.1.1.
The Person, Nārāyaṇa, desired: "May I transcend all beings; may I alone be all this.
He beheld this sacrificial rite of the Puruṣamedha lasting five nights; he took it up and performed it. Having sacrificed with it, he transcended all beings—this [all].

He transcends everything; he becomes all these beings; he becomes this entire universe—he who, knowing thus, performs the Puruṣamedha sacrifice, or whoever knows this thus. (13.6.1) For that [sacrifice], there are twenty-three initiation days (*dīkṣā*), twelve *upasad* days, and five pressing days (*sutyā*). Thus, it consists of forty nights.

Together with the *dīkṣā* and *upasads*, they consist of forty syllables; the *virāj* consists of forty syllables, and thus he attains the *virāj*. From that, the *virāj* was born; from the *virāj* was born the *puruṣa*. This indeed is that *virāj*; from this very *virāj* he thus generates the sacrifice, the *puruṣa*. These [stotras] consist of four decades; and as to why these consist of four decades, it is for the sake of these [worlds].
For the attainment of the worlds and the quarters, by the first decade they attained this very world,

by the second the intermediate space, by the third the sky, and by the fourth the quarters; in the same way, the sacrificer now attains this very world by the first decade, the intermediate space by the second, the sky by the third, and the quarters by the fourth— this much indeed [is it].
All this—these worlds and all the quarters—is the Puruṣamedha; it is for the attainment of everything, for the securing of everything.
On the day of preparation (upavasatha), there are eleven animals dedicated to Agni and Soma; their ritual procedure is the same, and there are eleven sacrificial posts (yūpa).

The *triṣṭubh* consists of eleven syllables; the *triṣṭubh* is a thunderbolt, and the *triṣṭubh* is vigor. By means of that very thunderbolt and that very vigor, the sacrificer repels evil from the front.
(13.6.1) At the Soma-pressings, there are animals for the eleven [deities]; the *triṣṭubh* consists of eleven syllables; the *triṣṭubh* is a thunderbolt, and the *triṣṭubh* is vigor.
By means of the *triṣṭubh* and by means of the thunderbolt, that is, by means of this very power, the sacrificer repels evil from the front.
Furthermore, as to why there are sets of eleven: the set of eleven is indeed this entire universe, for Prajāpati is the set of eleven;
and Prajāpati is everything, and the Puruṣamedha is everything—for the attainment of everything, for the securing of everything.

This Puruṣamedha, this sacrificial rite, consists of five nights; for sacrifice is fivefold, the animal victim is fivefold, there are five seasons, and the year is fivefold. Whatever is fivefold—whether concerning the deities or concerning the self—all that he attains by means of this. 13.6.1. [8]
Its first day is an Agniṣṭoma, then an Ukthya, then an Atirātra, then an Ukthya, and then an Agniṣṭoma.
This five-night sacrifice is indeed "lighted on both sides" and "Ukthya on both sides";
it is a Yavamadhyama (barley-shaped in the middle) Pañcarātra. These worlds are indeed the Puruṣamedha, for they are lighted on both sides.

These worlds are led by Agni from below and by Āditya from above; therefore, there is light on both sides. Food is the Ukthya, and the self is the Atirātra. Because these two Ukthyas are on both sides of the Atirātra, this self is encompassed by food.
And because this Atirātra is the longest of the days and is in the middle, it is therefore "yavamadhya" (barley-shaped in the middle); he who knows this indeed prospers.
"Verily, he who knows this has no hateful rival; they say of him, 'He has no hateful rival.

[13.6.1.10] Of this [sacrifice], this world is the first day; this world of his is the spring season. That which is above this world and below the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is the second day; that is his summer season.

The seasons [are as follows]: the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) itself is his middle day; the intermediate space is his [seasons of] the rainy season and autumn. That which is above the intermediate space and below the sky is his fourth day; that is his winter season. The sky itself is his fifth day; the sky is his dewy season (*śiśira*). This is with respect to the deities (*adhidevatam*). 13.6.1. [11]
Now, with respect to the self: his first day is indeed his foundation; the spring season is his foundation.
That which is above the foundation and below the middle constitutes his second day; that is his summer season. His middle day is indeed his middle;
the rainy and autumn seasons are his middle. That which is above...

That which is below the middle of the head is the fourth day; that is his winter season. His head itself is the fifth day; his head is his dewy season (*śiśira*). Thus these worlds, the year, and the self become the Puruṣamedha. Indeed, all these worlds are everything, and the year is everything.

The whole is the self; the Puruṣamedha is the whole, for the attainment of the whole and for the securing of the whole. 13.6.2. Now, as to why it is called Puruṣamedha: these worlds are indeed the city (*puri*), and this person (*puruṣa*) who blows here (the wind) lies within that city; therefore he is a *puruṣa*. Whatever food there is in these worlds, that is his food.

It is *medhas* because this food of his is *medhas*; therefore it is the *puruṣamedha*. Moreover, because he immolates sacrificial men (*medhya-puruṣa*) upon him, for that reason also it is the *puruṣamedha*. 13.6.2.
He immolates them on the middle day; for the middle day is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), and the intermediate space indeed—
Now, these animals are indeed the abode and the food of all beings;
the middle day is the belly, and thus he places that food within the belly.
He slaughters ten of each [kind of animal], for the *virāj* consists of ten syllables, and the *virāj* is the entirety of food.
For the attainment of all food, he sacrifices eleven animals at a time. The *triṣṭubh* consists of eleven syllables; the *triṣṭubh* is a thunderbolt, and the *triṣṭubh* is vigor.
By means of this thunderbolt and this vigor, the sacrificer strikes away evil from the middle.
He sacrifices forty-eight animals at the middle sacrificial post; the Jagatī meter has forty-eight syllables, and cattle are connected with the Jagatī;
verily by means of the Jagatī he secures cattle for him.
Eleven at each of the other posts; the Triṣṭubh has eleven syllables, and the Triṣṭubh is a thunderbolt, [the source of] vigor.
By means of the *triṣṭubh* and the thunderbolt, by that very power, the sacrificer repels evil on both sides.
He sacrifices eight animals last; the *gāyatrī* consists of eight syllables, and the *gāyatrī* is the Brahman.
Thus he makes the Brahman the highest of all this; therefore they say, "The Brahman is the highest of all this."
They indeed belong to Prajāpati; for Prajāpati is Brahman, since Prajāpati is of the nature of Brahman, therefore they belong to Prajāpati. 13.6.2.
[9] When he is about to dedicate the animals, he offers these three oblations to Savitṛ, O God.
"Of Savitṛ, that most excellent [gift] of Savitṛ..."—with these words he gratifies Savitṛ. He, being gratified, impels these persons for him;
impelled by him, he slaughters them.
He slaughters a Brāhmaṇa for the Brahman. The Brāhmaṇa is indeed the Brahman; thus, by means of the Brahman, he [slaughters] the Brahman.
He prospers the Rājanya for the sake of *kṣatra*; the Rājanya is indeed *kṣatra*, so he thus prospers *kṣatra* by means of *kṣatra*.
He [prospers] the Vaiśya for the sake of the Maruts; the Maruts are indeed the *viś*, so he thus prospers the *viś* by means of the *viś*.
He [prospers] the Śūdra for the sake of austerity (*tapas*); the Śūdra is indeed austerity, so he thus prospers austerity by means of austerity. Thus are these deities.

In whatever manner he causes prosperity through the sacrificial animals, they, being prosperous, cause him to prosper with all his desires. (13.6.2.11) He offers with clarified butter; clarified butter is indeed brilliance. By means of brilliance, he bestows that brilliance upon him. He offers with clarified butter; for clarified butter is the beloved abode of the gods. By means of this beloved abode, he causes them to prosper; they, in turn, [prosper him].

Prosperous, they prosper [the sacrificer] with all desires. 13.6.2.[12] Brahmā, standing to the south, praises the appointed men with the Puruṣa-sūkta, beginning with "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads,
a thousand eyes, a thousand feet"— with this hymn of sixteen verses, for this entire universe consists of sixteen parts.
"The Puruṣamedha is everything; it is for the attainment of everything, for the securing of everything.
Thus he praises him, thus he magnifies him, and moreover, he speaks of him as he truly is. Then the animals had the fire carried around them, but they were not yet slaughtered. 13.6.2. [13]

Then Speech addressed him, saying, "O Puruṣa, do not stop! If you stop, Puruṣa will devour Puruṣa. He released them after they had been encircled by fire and offered oblations to those respective deities. By these he gratified those deities, and they, being gratified, gratified him with all his desires. 13.6.2 [14]

He offers with clarified butter; clarified butter is indeed brilliance. Verily, by means of brilliance, he bestows brilliance upon him. (13.6.2.15) He concludes with the eleven-fold offerings. The Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables, and the Triṣṭubh is a thunderbolt; the Triṣṭubh is vigor.
By means of that very thunderbolt and that very vigor, the sacrificer strikes away evil from the middle. (13.6.2.16)
When the *udayanīyā* offering has been completed, he immolates eleven barren cows as *anūbandhya* victims:
those dedicated to Mitra-Varuṇa, those to the Viśve Devas, and those to Bṛhaspati; this is for the attainment of these deities.
As to why those dedicated to Bṛhaspati are last: Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; thus, he finally establishes himself in the Brahman. 13.6.2. [17]
Now there are eleven [verses]; the *triṣṭubh* consists of eleven syllables. The *triṣṭubh* is a thunderbolt (*vajra*), and the *triṣṭubh* is vigor.

By means of this thunderbolt and this vigor, the sacrificer strikes away evil from the middle. The *traidhātavī* is the concluding offering (*udavasānīyā*); its significance is the same as before. 13.6.2. [18]

Now, therefore, regarding the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*): from the middle of the kingdom, excluding what belongs to the land and the wealth of the Brahmin, [the remainder is divided]. The eastern quarter is for the *hotṛ*, the southern for the *udgātṛ*, the western for the *brahman*, and the northern for the *adhvaryu*. Those who have the office of the *hotṛ* (*hotṛka*) are likewise entitled to a share. 13.6.2. [19]
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, he should give away all his possessions (*sarvavedasa*); for the Brāhmaṇa is everything, and all his possessions are everything.
The Puruṣamedha is everything, for the attainment of everything and the securing of everything. 13.6.2.
[20] Then, having consigned the two fires into himself, ...

Having worshipped the sun with the Uttaranārāyaṇa hymn, he should depart for the forest without looking back; thus he becomes invisible to men. But if he should wish to dwell in a village, he should consign the two fires into the two kindling woods, worship the sun with the Uttaranārāyaṇa hymn itself, and settle down in his home. Then...

One should perform those sacrificial rites which one might be able to accomplish. Now, this [Puruṣamedha] is not to be recited for everyone, for the Puruṣamedha is everything; [one should think], "Lest I speak everything to just anyone. One should indeed recite it only for one who is well-known, or for one who is learned in the Vedas, or for one who is dear to him—but by no means to just anyone. 13.7.1. [1]

Brahman, indeed, the Self-existent, performed austerity. Then he reflected: "There is indeed no infinity in austerity; come now, let me offer myself as a sacrifice in all beings, and all beings in myself. Having offered himself in all beings and all beings in himself, he attained preeminence, sovereignty, and lordship over all beings.
In the same way, the sacrificer at the Sarvamedha, having offered all sacrifices, passes beyond all beings to preeminence, self-sovereignty, and lordship.
This Sarvamedha indeed consists of a ten-night sacrificial session; the Virāj has ten syllables, and the Virāj is...

The entire food is for the sake of securing the entirety of what is to be eaten. Upon it he piles the fire-altar as the highest; for the Sarvamedha is the highest of sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*). By means of the highest, he causes him to reach the highest state. 13.7.1. [3] Its first day is the Agniṣṭut Agniṣṭoma; for Agni indeed...
The Agniṣṭut is an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. All the gods indeed have Agni as their mouth; it is for the attainment of all the gods.
Its cups belong to Agni, and its *puroruc* verses belong to Agni, so that everything may be dedicated to Agni.
The second day is an Ukthya sacrifice dedicated to Indra. Indra, indeed, is all the gods; [it is for the attainment of all the gods].

For the attainment of the gods, there are cups for Indra; the *puroruc* verses are addressed to Indra, so that everything may belong to Indra. 13.7.1.[5] The third day is an Ukthya sacrifice for Sūrya. Sūrya indeed is all the gods; it is for the attainment of all the gods that there are cups for Sūrya; the *puroruc* verses are addressed to Sūrya, so that everything may belong to Sūrya. 13.7.1.[6]
The fourth day is the Vaiśvadeva; for the Viśve are all the gods, and it serves to attain all the gods.
There are Vaiśvadeva cups, and there are Vaiśvadeva *paroruca* verses, so that everything may be Vaiśvadeva.
The fifth day, the middle one, belongs to the Aśvamedha; on that day, the horse [is released].

He sacrifices a victim for the Medhya; this is for the attainment of the Aśvamedha itself. 13.7.1.[8] The middle sixth day belongs to the Puruṣamedha; on that day he sacrifices men fit for sacrifice, for the attainment of the Puruṣamedha itself. 13.7.1.[9]
The Aptyoryāma is the seventh day, for the attainment of all sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*).
On that day, he immolates all animals fit for sacrifice—whatever is animate and whatever is inanimate. Of those possessing omenta, he offers the omentum;
of those without omenta, he cuts off the skin. They scatter the cuttings of herbs and trees, both dry and fresh.

He offers food after food from the moist substances for the attainment of every kind of food; he offers everything, he offers for the sake of everything, for the attainment of everything, and for the securing of everything. Just as it is at the morning pressing when the omenta have been offered, so it is at the third pressing when the oblations have been offered. 13.7.1. [10]
The thirteenth day is the Triṇava; the Triṇava is indeed the thunderbolt (vajra), and by the thunderbolt, indeed, the kṣatra is won.

Thus, by means of the thunderbolt itself, he wins the kṣatra. The fourteenth day is the Trayastriṃśa; the Trayastriṃśa is indeed a firm foundation (pratiṣṭhā). It serves for the sake of establishing a firm foundation.

The tenth day is the Viśvajit Atirātra with all the Pṛṣṭhas. Indeed, the Viśvajit Atirātra with all the Pṛṣṭhas is everything; the Sarvamedha is everything. It is for the attainment of everything, for the securing of everything.
Now, therefore, regarding the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās): up to the center of the kingdom, including whatever else belongs to a Brāhmaṇa’s wealth along with the land.

The eastern quarter belongs to the Hotṛ together with his man; the southern to the Brahman; the western to the Adhvaryu; and the northern to the Udgātṛ. In that very same way, the minor Hotṛ-priests are included. With this [sacrifice], Viśvakarman Bhauvana performed a sacrifice; having sacrificed with it, he surpassed all beings here.
It has become everything; it transcends all beings; it becomes this entire universe for one who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Sarvamedha, or who knows this thus. 13.7.1.
Kaśyapa performed that sacrifice for him, and regarding this, the Earth sang a verse: "No mortal whatsoever [can surpass me]..."
"O Viśvakarman Bhauvana, you ought to give [this]. You have been slow, O Upamañghri; you were in the midst of the waters.
This promise of yours to Kaśyapa was in vain.
Then they perform auspicious rites for him; then they prepare a burial mound (*śmaśāna*) for him, or a house, or a memorial monument (*prajñāna*). Whoever...
Whoever dies is a corpse (*śava*); for him he prepares this food. Therefore it is called *śavānna* (corpse-food).

They call it *śmaśāna* cryptically; for *śmaśā* is indeed the name of the eaters of the ancestors (*pitṛs*). They seize the merit of one who has not prepared a *śmaśāna* in that world; for them, this food [is prepared].
Therefore, he makes it a *śmaśāna* (burial ground); for that which is a *śmaśāna* they call "the burial ground" (*śmaśānam*) cryptically (*parokṣam*).
He should not do it quickly, thinking, "Lest I make fresh evil. He should do it after a long time; thus he makes that evil distant.
Where even his kin no longer remember him, there he causes that evil to go to utter oblivion.

If they should remember [the proper time], one should perform it in odd-numbered years; for the ancestors belong to the odd-numbered [years]. Under a single lunar mansion (*ekanakṣatra*), for the ancestors belong to a single lunar mansion. On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), there is a single lunar mansion; indeed, the new moon day is a single lunar mansion, for on that night all [the stars] are one.
All beings dwell together with him; therefore, he obtains that desire who [performs this] among all the lunar mansions.
(13.8.1[4]) One should perform it in autumn, for autumn is indeed *svadhā*, and *svadhā* is the food of the ancestors; thus he places him in food, in *svadhā*.
Or [one may perform it] in Māgha, thinking, "May no evil come to us"; or in summer, thinking, "May evil be laid low for us. (13.8.1[5])

The four-cornered [altars] belong to both the gods and the asuras, the offspring of Prajāpati; they contended for the quarters. Those gods drove their rivals, the asuras, from the quarters; being deprived of the quarters, the asuras were defeated.
Therefore, those divine offspring who construct four-cornered burial mounds (śmaśāna) prosper, whereas those asura offspring do not even today [construct them].
They indeed measured them out from you as circular; he places them between both directions, the eastern and the southern.
For in this direction lies the gate of the world of the Fathers; by means of that very gate, he causes him to enter the world of the Fathers.
By its corners he becomes firmly established in the cardinal directions, and by its other body in the intermediate directions; thus he establishes him in all the directions.
He establishes it. 13.8.1.[6] Now, therefore, regarding the selection of the ground: he prepares it on ground sloping toward the north. The north is indeed the direction of men;
thus he causes him to partake in the world of men. For the ancestors partake in the world of men in this very way, namely, when [the ground] belongs to them.

Offspring is born; indeed, his offspring becomes more excellent. 13.8.1.[7] "One should perform it on ground sloping toward the south," they say, "for the world of the ancestors slopes toward the south; thus he grants him a share in the world of the ancestors.
One should not do so; for that making of a cemetery is truly called "the bringer of disease," and it quickly [brings it about].
Another [person] follows after them.
Regarding this, some say that one should perform the rite on ground sloping toward the south, for "in that way, the evil is turned back.
But one should not do it so; rather, when one performs it on ground sloping toward the north, in that very way the evil is turned back.

If, while he is thus levelled, water should come from the south-east, flow around him, and reach this direction without striking him, so that he might attain inexhaustible waters—he should perform that rite. For water is indeed food; he thereby places food before him facing westward. And water is indeed immortality; he is thus the life of living beings.

The rising of the seven seers in the direction of the horizon and the setting of the sun—that is indeed immortality; he bestows that very immortality upon the living beings. This making of the burial mound is called *pratimīvat*; it is beneficial for the living. Indeed, what is beneficial for the living is also beneficial for the ancestors. 13.8.1 [10]
One should make it pleasant, thinking, "May there be pleasure for me"; and one should make it auspicious, thinking, "May there be well-being for me.
One should not make it on a public road, nor in the open air, lest one make one's sin manifest.
It may be hidden even though it is accessible; in that it is hidden, one hides one's very sin. Then...
Or, since that sun is the remover of evil, it removes evil from him; moreover, it makes him possessed of the light of the sun.
One should not do this for one whose rear is thus exposed, for that is called "begging," and it leads to swift [misfortune].
Another follows after them: there should be something variegated behind;
for offspring are indeed variegated, and his offspring will be variegated. If there were nothing variegated, there should be water behind or on the north; for water is indeed variegated.
His offspring indeed becomes such [as he desires].
He performs it on saline soil; saline earth is seed, it is procreation; thus he causes him to participate in procreation.
For the ancestors indeed participate in procreation when they have offspring; his offspring will be even more excellent.
[It] comes to be.

13.8.1.[15] [If he offers it] with the roots, [it is] indeed with the roots for the ancestors; this is mixed with *vīriṇa* grass, for this is his ancestral portion, not excessive, and furthermore, he thereby binds that very evil. 13.8.1.[16]
One should not place the *bhūmipāśa* plant there, nor the *śara*, nor the *aśmagandhā*, nor the *adhyāṇḍā*, nor the *pṛśniparṇī*.

One should not have [the fire] near an *aśvattha* tree, nor a *vibhītaka*, nor a *tilvaka*, nor a *sphūrjaka*, nor a *haridrā*, nor a *nyagrodha*; and whatever other trees have evil names, one should avoid them by name alone out of a desire for auspiciousness.
For the sake of avoidance, 13.8.1.[17]:

Now, therefore, according to the procedure for the fire-altar, he constructs the burial mound (*śmaśāna*) for the one who has piled the fire-altar. For when the sacrificer piles the fire-altar, he thereby prepares himself by means of the sacrifice for that world; this indeed is the sacrificial element.

The rite remains incomplete until the construction of the cremation ground; thus, when he constructs the cremation ground for one who has piled the fire-altar according to the rules for the fire-piling, he thereby brings that very fire-piling to completion.
One should not make it too large, thinking, "Lest I commit a great evil."
"An altar as large as the fire with its wings and tail would wear out," so say some, "for this body of his is the same as that of the fire.
One should, however, make it merely man-sized; thus one does not leave space for another behind, and offspring increase further. 13.8.1 [19]

Verily, by doing so, they make their offspring more excellent; on the north side [they make it] broader, for offspring are indeed superior; thus he makes his offspring more excellent. Having thus arranged it, he encloses it with cords twisted from right to left, for the rite of the ancestors is performed from right to left. 13.8.1. [20]
Then he says to the excavator: "He should dig as much as he intends to pour; however, he should dig to the height of a man.

In this way, he leaves no room for another. Moreover, the world of the Pitṛs is indeed the world of plants, and they creep toward the roots of the plants. Furthermore, [he does so] lest it be hidden within her. 13.8.2. [1]
Some bury [the bones] after they have disappeared. Both the gods and the Asuras, the offspring of Prajāpati, contended for this world.
Those gods drove out their rivals, the Asuras, from this world;
therefore, those who are divine creatures prepare burial grounds that are not hidden, whereas those who are of the nature of the Asuras prepare those that are hidden away.
"On this earth, from you"—thus [he says].
Then he encloses it with the enclosing-stones (*pariśrit*). Those which are those [other] enclosing-stones, those he encloses with a sacrificial formula (*yajus*);

these he encloses silently. He thus distinguishes between that which belongs to the gods and that which belongs to the fathers. He uses an unlimited number [of stones], for that world is indeed unlimited.
Then he sweeps it away with a Palāśa branch; that which was the sweeping away at the beginning is this very act.

With the words, "Let the Paṇis go away, the ill-minded ones who revile the gods," he thus drives away from this world the Paṇis, those ill-minded revilers of the gods, the Asuras and Rakṣasas; for this world belongs to him.

"Of him who has pressed [the Soma]"—for he who has sacrificed is indeed one who has pressed; "by days, by nights, by the seasons, clearly"—thereby he makes him share the same world with the seasons and the days and nights.
"May Yama grant us a dwelling"—Yama, indeed, rules over this dwelling; it is to him that he [grants it] for him.
He asks for a place to rest; he throws that [stick] toward the south and the other toward the north, thereby distinguishing between the divine and the ancestral rites.
Then he yokes the plough from the south; some say from the north, but let him do as he desires.

Having given the command, "Yoke [the oxen]," he consecrates [the oxen] with the mantra: "May Savitṛ seek a place on earth for your bodies. Indeed, Savitṛ himself seeks a place on earth for his bodies. [He continues: "Let the oxen be yoked for him," for it is for this rite that the oxen are yoked. 13.8.2. [6]

It consists of six oxen; there are six seasons in the year. Thus he establishes him in the seasons, in the year, as his foundation. Having turned it counter-clockwise, he ploughs the first furrow on the north side facing west with the mantra, "May Vāyu purify [it]. With the mantra, "With the brilliance," he ploughs the southern half with the southern fire-altar.

With the formula, "The eastern [furrow] with the splendor of the sun," he plows first toward the north along the front. He plows four furrows with a *yajus* formula; thus, whatever food exists in the four quarters, he establishes him therein. Indeed, it is by means of a *yajus*; for the *yajus* is truly the truth (*addhā*). It is indeed the truth.

Then, as for these directions: he draws himself [toward them]. Whatever food there is in the year, therein he thus establishes him. He does so silently with an unlimited number of [draws], for that world is unlimited.

Then he unyokes it after having performed that rite for which he had yoked it, with the formula, "May the cows be unyoked," for it is for this very rite that the cows are yoked. He throws it toward the south, and the other [cord] toward the north; thus he distinguishes between what belongs to the gods and what belongs to the fathers. 13.8.3.1.

Then he sows all kinds of herbs. That same all-herb mixture which was previously [sown] with many [verses], he now sows with a single verse; thus he distinguishes between that which belongs to the gods and that which belongs to the fathers. With the words, "In the *aśvattha* tree is your seat, on the *parṇa* leaf is your dwelling," he thereby prays for long life for them. And so it is.
"One after another of these follows the other in death through old age.
Then he pours him out; this earth is indeed the foundation, and thus he establishes him upon this very foundation.
Before the rising of the sun—he does so while it is still dark, for the fathers are as if hidden, and the night is as if hidden; thus he makes it hidden.
Just as it might rise upon one who is performing [the rite], so he establishes him in both the day and the night.

"May Savitṛ cast thy limbs into the lap of the Mother," he says; thus Savitṛ himself casts his limbs into the lap of this earth, the Mother. "Be auspicious to her, O Earth," he says, so that she may be auspicious to him.
"It may be so," he says; "I place you in the deity Prajāpati, in the world near the water, O So-and-so!"—thus he takes his name.
This world indeed is the one near the water; thus he places him in the deity Prajāpati, in the world near the water.
Then he says to someone: "Go in this direction without looking back, and having gone until the jar is exhausted, come back."

There he mutters: "O Death, go along the other path, which is yours and different from the path of the gods; I speak to you who have eyes and hear: do not harm our offspring nor our heroes. He thus prays for long life for them; accordingly, one by one of them passes away only when overtaken by old age. 13.8.3 [5]
Then he arranges it limb by limb: "May the wind be auspicious for you; may the heat of the sun be auspicious for you; may the bricks be auspicious for you;
may the earthly fires be auspicious for you—let them not consume you. May the quarters be fit for you; may the waters be most propitious to you;
may the rivers be propitious to you; may the atmosphere be auspicious for you; may the quarters be fit for you."
"Everything"—this indeed prepares everything for him; this makes it auspicious for him.
(13.8.3[6]) Then, thirteen unmarked bricks the size of a foot are prepared. Those which are the fire-bricks (*agniṣṭakā*) are these [other bricks];
he lays those down with a *yajus* formula, and these silently. Thus he distinguishes between that which belongs to the gods and that which belongs to the ancestors. (13.8.3[7])

There are thirteen; there are thirteen months in a year. Thus, he establishes him in the seasons, in the year, which is the foundation. (13.8.3) They are a foot in measure; the foot is indeed a foundation. He thus provides a foundation for him. They are markless.
The ancestors are indeed hidden; that which is without a mark is hidden, so he places it in a hidden manner.

Of those [bricks], he places one in the middle facing east—that is the body (*ātman*). Three are placed in front, joined at the head—that is the head (*śiras*). Three are on the south—that is the right wing (*pakṣa*). Three are on the north—that is the... [left wing].

The northern side consists of three [bricks]; that is its tail. Thus this self of his possesses wings and a tail, just as that of Agni. 13.8.3. Now, he says, "One should bring the loose soil from a cleft," for that is its ancestral portion, not an addition; moreover, he thereby makes it firm. However, some dig a trench in an intermediate direction and bring the soil from there.
Some indeed drag [the fire] from the south, then from the west, then from the north, and from there they bring it forward; he may do as he desires.
One should not make it too large, thinking, "Lest I should commit a great evil"; it should be as large as one's outstretched arms.

A man should make [the sacrificial post] as high as the mouth for a Kṣatriya, as high as the genitals for a Brāhmaṇa, as high as the thighs for a woman, and as high as the knees for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra; for such is their respective strength.
However, one should rather make it below the knee, so that it does not leave space for another while it is being made.
They hold the *tejanī* (a bundle of reeds) to the north; for that is offspring (*prajā*), and thus they hold offspring to the north.
Having taken it up, or having carried it, one should set it upright in the house; thereby one sets offspring upright in the house.
(13.8.3) Having performed [the rite], he sows barley, saying, "May you drive away (*yavaya*) my evil. He covers it with *avakā* plants, thinking, "May there be pleasure (*kam*) for me."
He covers it with *darbha* grass for the sake of non-aridity.

Then he fixes it around with stakes: one made of *palāśa* wood to the east; the *palāśa* is indeed the Brahman, so he causes it to go to the heavenly world with the Brahman as its leader. One made of *śamī* wood to the north; *śamī* is peace (*śam*).

"May it ward off evil from me"—with this he places a barrier behind; "may it ward off evil from me"—with this he places the *vṛtra-śaṅku* (Vṛtra-pike) to the south, so that evil may not pass beyond. 13.8.4.
[2] Then, to the south, they dig two curved trenches (*parivakra*) and fill them with milk and water.
When he has reached that world, they run toward him at two streams; seven [streams] fill them with water.
Indeed, one cannot cross over the seven flowing rivers, so as not to pass beyond evil (agha).
They scatter three stones each; they cross over them, [saying]: "The stony one flows. 13.8.4. [3]
"Exert yourselves! Arise! Cross over, O friends! Here let us leave behind those who are inauspicious;
may we, being auspicious, cross over toward strengths"—as the *yajus* is, so is its significance.
(13.8.4) With *apāmārga* plants they wipe away; they thus wipe away evil, they wipe away sin, they wipe away misfortune, and they wipe away sorcery.
"O Apāmārga, drive away from us the evil dream," he says; as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance.
13.8.4 [5] Where there is water, they bathe there. "May the waters and plants be friendly to us," with these words he takes up water in his joined palms.
Water is indeed a thunderbolt; by means of the thunderbolt he thus establishes friendship, while for that [enemy] may they be unfriendly.
Whoever hates us, and whomsoever we hate—he indeed causes that person to perish.

(13.8.4) If the waters are still, they cause the evil of these people to stand still; and if they flow, they carry away the evil of these people. Having bathed and put on washed garments, [they mount] oxen.

Holding onto the tail, they proceed; for the ox belongs to Agni, and thus they proceed from the world of the fathers to the world of the living with Agni at their head. Moreover, Agni is the one who carries across the path;
he carries them across. Reciting this verse, "Up from out of the darkness," they go; that is, from the darkness of the world of the fathers, [they go] toward the sun.
They proceed toward the light; when they have arrived, they offer them collyrium and ointment.
This is human adornment; by means of it, they conceal that death. 13.8.4.
Then, having established the fire in the house and having laid down enclosing-sticks of *vāraṇa* wood, [they offer] to the fire with a *sruva* ladle made of *vāraṇa* wood.

He offers an oblation for the long-lived one; Agni, indeed, is long-lived and rules over life. He thus begs life from him [Agni] with the verse, "O Agni, you purify lives," which serves as the portion for the invitatory formula (*puro'nuvākyā*).
Then he offers: "O Agni, long-lived, increasing by the oblation, with ghee as your face and ghee as your womb, come; having drunk the ghee..."
"Sweet and pleasant is the milk of the cow; protect these as a father protects his son, saying 'Svāhā!'"—by this he says exactly how one should protect them and how one should guard them.
An old ox is its sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), as well as old barley and a bench with a cushion; this is indeed the prescribed [fee].
"One may give more sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) at will, according to one's faith," so they say regarding the piler of the fire-altar (agnicit).

Now, for one who does not pile the fire-altar: this very choosing of the ground is the same; he should perform whatever ritual action other than that of the fire-altar belongs to one who has established the sacred fires.

Regarding this, some say: "The pebbles are those of the one who has established the fires," meaning these are the very same pebbles used at the establishment of the fires (agnyādheya); [but others say] "no."
"One [should] do so," says one [teacher], "lest these [fires] scorch one who has not built the fire-altar. He may act as he desires.

Having taken a clod of earth from the boundary-line itself, he places it between [the fires], saying: "I set up this enclosure for the living, so that no other may reach this goal of theirs; may they live a hundred abundant autumns, keeping death within."
With the words, "May they uphold it with the mountain," he establishes this boundary for both the living and the ancestors so that there may be no confusion;
therefore, indeed, the living and the ancestors do not see one another.
